title: Criminal Law
topics: Structure of criminal law; actus reus, mens rea

notes.h: Building blocks: actus reus, mens rea and the burden of proof
notes.body:
Most offences combine an actus reus (the external elements) and a mens rea (the fault element), with no defence available. The prosecution must prove every element beyond reasonable doubt, the 'golden thread' of Woolmington v DPP [1935], subject to insanity and statutory reverse burdens.

Actus reus
- Elements are conduct, circumstances and, for result crimes, a consequence. A conduct crime (e.g. fraud by false representation, s2 Fraud Act 2006) needs no outcome; a result crime (e.g. murder) does.
- Conduct must be voluntary, although situational offences such as R v Larsonneur (1933) and Winzar v CC of Kent (1983) are criticised for punishing involuntary states.

Mens rea
It is assessed element by element: intention, recklessness, knowledge, belief or dishonesty. The principle of correspondence says fault should match each element. Constructive offences break it, such as s47 OAPA 1861, unlawful act manslaughter and the GBH form of murder.

Coincidence
Actus reus and mens rea must coincide, but the courts are flexible.
- Continuing act: Fagan v MPC [1969], car left on a constable's foot.
- Series of acts: Thabo Meli v R [1954], where the plan to kill and the later disposal of the 'body' were treated as one transaction.

Transferred malice
Mens rea transfers to an unintended victim of the same offence (R v Latimer (1886)) but not between different offences (R v Pembliton (1874)). D who aims at a person and breaks a window may still be reckless as to the window under R v G [2003].

Strict liability
Where a statute is silent, mens rea is presumed (Sweet v Parsley [1970]), including as to age (B v DPP [2000]). The presumption may be displaced, for example for regulatory offences protecting public safety (Gammon v AG of Hong Kong [1985]), as in Pharmaceutical Society v Storkwain [1986]. Supporters cite efficiency and deterrence; critics stress punishment of the blameless.

Worked example: Rhys strikes Tom intending to kill, believes him dead and rolls him into a river, where he drowns. Under Thabo Meli the acts form one transaction, so murder is made out. Later he throws a glass at Vic, which hits Wendy and then shatters a mirror: malice transfers to Wendy's injury. It does not transfer to the mirror; criminal damage depends on Rhys's own recklessness, which he denies.

Exam pitfalls
- Transferring malice from a person to property.
- Forgetting the presumption of mens rea before calling an offence strict.
- Treating motive as mens rea.

Omissions
There is no general duty to act. Liability for an omission needs (i) an offence capable of commission by omission and (ii) a recognised duty:
- contract: R v Pittwood (1902), level-crossing gatekeeper;
- voluntary assumption of care: R v Stone and Dobinson [1977];
- creating a dangerous situation: R v Miller [1983], extended in R v Evans [2009] to contributing to a known life-threatening state;
- special relationships and statute.
Withdrawing life-sustaining treatment was treated as an omission, lawful where continued treatment is not in the patient's best interests (Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993]); critics call the act/omission line artificial.

Causation
- Factual: but for D's conduct, would the result have occurred? R v White [1910], where poison did not cause the death.
- Legal: D's conduct must be a more than minimal, operating cause (R v Pagett (1983)).
- Medical treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent and potent that D's contribution becomes insignificant (R v Cheshire [1991]).
- A victim's escape breaks it only if 'daft' or unforeseeable (R v Roberts (1971)).
- Thin skull rule: D takes V as he finds her, beliefs included (R v Blaue [1975]).
- A free, deliberate and informed act of an adult breaks the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007]).

Recklessness
Under R v G [2003], D is reckless if aware of a risk that a circumstance exists or a result will occur and, in the circumstances known to him, it is unreasonable to take it. This subjective test overruled the objective Caldwell [1982] test, whose harshness showed in Elliott v C (1983).

Worked example: Gemma agrees to care for her frail uncle and stops feeding him and giving his medication. He falls, and in hospital a doctor carelessly gives a drug to which he is allergic; he dies of pneumonia. Gemma owed a duty by assuming care (Stone and Dobinson) and by agreement. The doctor's negligence is unlikely to break the chain under Cheshire because Gemma's neglect remained an operating and significant cause. Gross negligence manslaughter then turns on the Adomako test.

Exam pitfalls
- Citing Miller for a duty without showing D became aware of the danger.
- Treating any medical negligence as breaking the chain.
- Describing Caldwell recklessness as current law.
- Forgetting that Kennedy concerns self-administration by a fully informed adult.

The Criminal Damage Act 1971 creates the main property-damage offences.

Basic offence: s1(1)
Without lawful excuse, destroying or damaging property belonging to another, intending to or being reckless (R v G [2003]) as to the damage and as to the property belonging to another. Maximum 10 years.
- 'Damage' is a question of fact and degree: physical harm or impairment of value or usefulness, even if temporary. Water-soluble paint on a pavement (Hardman [1986]) and a flooded cell blanket (R v Fiak [2005]) counted; a scratch on a scaffold bar did not (Morphitis v Salmon [1990]).
- 'Property' (s10) is tangible property, including land and tamed animals, excluding wild mushrooms, flowers, fruit and foliage and anything intangible.
- An honest belief that the property is one's own, even through a mistake of civil law, negates mens rea (R v Smith (David) [1974]).

Aggravated offence: s1(2)
Damaging any property, including one's own, with intention or recklessness as to the damage and as to whether life would thereby be endangered. Life need not actually be endangered, but the danger must come from the damage, not from the missile (R v Steer [1988]). Maximum life; the s5 excuses do not apply.

Arson: s1(3). Damage by fire under s1(1) or s1(2), maximum life.

Lawful excuse: s5
- s5(2)(a): belief that the owner consented or would have consented. Honest belief suffices (s5(3)), even if drunken (Jaggard v Dickinson [1981]).
- s5(2)(b): acting to protect property believed to be in immediate need of protection, by means believed reasonable. The beliefs are subjective, but whether D acted 'in order to protect property' is objective (R v Hill and Hall (1989)).
- Protest: Convention rights to expression and assembly do not provide a defence where significant damage is caused (AG's Reference (No 1 of 2022), the Colston statue case).

Worked example: Lena saws a lock off a bike she wrongly thinks is hers. Smith (David) negates mens rea. Her chalked protest slogans that cost £300 to jet-wash are probably damage under Hardman. Smashing a car window to save a dog she believes is dying may be excused under s5(2)(b) if she believed the dog (property) needed immediate protection and the means were reasonable. Her honest but mistaken belief can suffice.

Exam pitfalls
- Charging s1(1) for damage to D's own property: use s1(2) if life is endangered.
- Asking whether the bullet, rather than the broken glass, endangered life.
- Applying s5 excuses to the aggravated offence.
- Forgetting that a drunken belief can still found s5(2)(a).

notes.h: Non-fatal offences against the person and consent
notes.body:
Offences rise in seriousness from assault to s18.

The offences
- Assault: causing V to apprehend immediate unlawful force, intentionally or recklessly. Words or silence can suffice, and 'immediate' can include within a minute or two (R v Ireland [1998]). Charged under s39 CJA 1988.
- Battery: intentional or reckless application of unlawful force, however slight. Everyday contact is impliedly consented to (Collins v Wilcock [1984]).
- s47 OAPA 1861: assault or battery occasioning ABH, meaning harm more than transient or trifling (R v Miller [1954]; R v Donovan [1934]), including brief unconsciousness (T v DPP [2003]) and cutting hair (DPP v Smith [2006]). Mens rea is only that for the assault or battery (R v Savage; DPP v Parmenter [1992]).
- s20: unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting GBH, foreseeing some harm (R v Mowatt [1968]). GBH means really serious harm (DPP v Smith [1961]) or serious harm (R v Saunders [1985]), assessed in light of V's age and health (R v Bollom [2003]). A wound breaks the whole skin (JCC v Eisenhower [1984]). Serious psychiatric injury counts, and infliction needs no direct force (R v Burstow [1998]).
- s18: wounding or causing GBH with intent to cause GBH (or to resist arrest). Maximum life.

Consent
Consent is a defence to assault and battery, but not to ABH or worse unless a public-interest exception applies (R v Brown [1994], 3–2). Exceptions include properly conducted sport (R v Barnes [2004]), surgery, tattooing, horseplay (R v Jones (1986); R v Aitken [1992]) and consensual branding between spouses (R v Wilson [1996]). R v Emmett [1999] fell outside them. Consent to the risk of HIV infection must be informed (R v Dica [2004]; R v Konzani [2005]). Section 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 puts the 'rough sex' position on a statutory footing. Non-fatal strangulation is a separate offence (s75A Serious Crime Act 2015), with the consent defence excluded where V suffers serious harm and D intended or was reckless as to it (s75A(3)).

Worked example: Pete's beer glass slips and cuts Rosa's forehead. Throwing beer over Rosa is an intended battery, and under Savage that mens rea suffices for s47; a cut needing stitches is a wound and ABH. For s20, Pete must foresee some harm, so if he never imagined the glass leaving his hand, s47 is safer. Punching a door supervisor and breaking his nose is at least s47, probably s20 if the injury is serious.

Exam pitfalls
- Requiring foresight of ABH for s47.
- Requiring foresight of serious harm for s20.
- Calling every injury GBH; consider V's characteristics.
- Treating Wilson as a general exception for private consensual harm.

Murder
The unlawful killing of a human being under the King's peace with malice aforethought, meaning an intention to kill or to cause GBH (R v Vickers [1957]; R v Cunningham [1982]). It carries a mandatory life sentence. A foetus is not a person, and malice cannot be transferred twice (AG's Reference (No 3 of 1994) [1998]).

Intention
- Direct intention: the result is D's aim or purpose.
- Oblique intention: the jury may find intention only if death or serious harm was a virtual certainty from D's act and D appreciated that (R v Nedrick [1986], approved in R v Woollin [1999], which changed 'infer' to 'find').
- Foresight is evidence of intention, not intention itself (R v Moloney [1985]). Woollin is a rule of evidence that permits, but does not compel, a finding (R v Matthews and Alleyne [2003]). Foresight of high probability (Hyam v DPP [1975]) is no longer enough.

Unlawful act manslaughter
- A deliberate act that is itself a crime, with its own mens rea (R v Lamb [1967]).
- Objectively dangerous: sober and reasonable people would see the risk of some harm (R v Church [1966]). The bystander knows what D knew or would have learned during the act (R v Dawson (1985) against R v Watson [1989]).
- It causes death. No foresight of harm is required (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977]). Self-injection by an informed adult breaks the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007]).

Gross negligence manslaughter
Duty, breach, causation of death and negligence so bad the jury considers it criminal (R v Adomako [1995]). The serious and obvious risk of death must be reasonably foreseeable on the information available at the time of breach (R v Rose [2017]).

Worked example: Uma pours petrol through a letterbox 'to scare' Viktor, and his son dies. Her purpose was not death, so the jury must be directed under Woollin: they may find intention to kill or cause GBH only if serious harm was virtually certain and she appreciated that. Her belief that the smoke alarm would wake them goes to whether she appreciated it. If intention is not found, unlawful act manslaughter (arson, obviously dangerous) is the fallback.

Reform
The Law Commission (2006) proposed a graded structure of homicide offences. Critics argue the GBH rule breaks the correspondence principle and the mandatory sentence prevents fine distinctions between killers.

Exam pitfalls
- Telling the jury foresight equals intention.
- Asking whether D foresaw harm for unlawful act manslaughter.
- Giving the reasonable bystander knowledge D could not have had.

Theft (s1 Theft Act 1968) is dishonestly appropriating property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it. Maximum 7 years.

Elements
- Appropriation (s3): any assumption of an owner's rights, and one right is enough (R v Morris [1984]). Consent is irrelevant (Lawrence v MPC [1972]; DPP v Gomez [1993]), and even receiving a valid gift can be appropriation (R v Hinks [2001]).
- Property (s4): confidential information is not property (Oxford v Moss (1978)).
- Belonging to another (s5): anyone with possession or control, so an owner can steal his own car from a garage (R v Turner (No 2) [1971]). s5(3) covers property received under an obligation to deal with it in a particular way (R v Hall [1973], none proved); s5(4) covers property got by mistake that D must restore (AG's Ref (No 1 of 1983), overpaid wages).
- Dishonesty: first s2(1). D is not dishonest if he believes he has a legal right, that the owner would consent, or that the owner cannot be found by reasonable steps. Willingness to pay is not decisive (s2(2)). Otherwise the jury finds D's actual belief about the facts and asks whether his conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people (Ivey v Genting [2017]; R v Barton and Booth [2020], replacing Ghosh's subjective limb).
- Intention to permanently deprive (s6): borrowing counts only if the thing is returned with its goodness or virtue gone (R v Lloyd [1985]).

Robbery (s8)
Stealing, and immediately before or at the time and in order to steal, using or threatening force. Slight force suffices (R v Clouden [1987]). Appropriation can be continuing (R v Hale (1978)). No theft means no robbery (R v Robinson [1977]). Maximum life.

Burglary (s9)
s9(1)(a): entering as a trespasser intending to steal, inflict GBH or do unlawful damage. s9(1)(b): having entered as a trespasser, stealing or inflicting GBH, or attempting to. Entry need only be effective (R v Brown [1985]); partial entry can suffice (R v Ryan (1996)).

Worked example: Bea takes £20 from the till meaning to replace it on Friday. She intends to return equivalent money, not the same note, so the intention to permanently deprive is present; dishonesty is for the jury under Ivey. Taking a named umbrella when there is a lost property box defeats any s2(1)(c) belief. Borrowing a book for the weekend lacks intention to permanently deprive.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying consent prevents appropriation after Gomez.
- Applying the Ghosh test.
- Forgetting that a belief in a legal right negates both theft and robbery.

The Fraud Act 2006 creates a single offence of fraud (s1), committable in three ways, with a maximum of 10 years. Each needs dishonesty (the Ivey test) and an intention to make a gain or cause loss, or expose another to a risk of loss.

The three forms
- s2, false representation: a representation of fact or law, including about a state of mind, express or implied, and possibly made to a machine (s2(3)–(5)). It is false if untrue or misleading and D knows it is or might be.
- s3, failing to disclose information D is under a legal duty to disclose. The duty may come from statute, contract, a fiduciary relationship or custom; a purely moral duty is not enough.
- s4, abuse of position: D occupies a position in which he is expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests, and dishonestly abuses it, possibly by omission. The position need not be fiduciary (R v Valujevs [2014], gangmasters).

Key features
- Fraud is a conduct crime. Nobody need be deceived, nothing need be obtained and no actual gain or loss is needed.
- Gain and loss (s5) mean money or other property only, temporary or permanent, and include keeping what one has or not getting what one might.
- Implied representations from older deception cases remain useful: using a cheque or credit card implies authority to use it (MPC v Charles [1977]; R v Lambie [1982]). Sitting in a restaurant is a continuing representation of intention to pay (DPP v Ray [1974]).

Related offences
- s11, obtaining services dishonestly: a result crime requiring the services to be obtained without full payment. Maximum 5 years.
- ss6–7: possessing, making or supplying articles for use in fraud.

Worked example: Faye sells counterfeit bags as 'authentic'. That is s2 fraud when she makes the statement, even if a buyer knows the truth, because no one need be deceived. Using a found debit card contactlessly is a false implied representation of authority, made to a machine (s2(5)). Transferring £5,000 from a neighbour's account under a power of attorney, meaning to repay, is potentially s4 abuse of position, and the jury decides dishonesty under Ivey. Failing to tell her landlord about her business, as required by her lease, may be s3 fraud if she intended gain or loss.

Criticism
By dropping deception, obtaining and loss, the Act pushes liability to an early stage and makes the jury's view of dishonesty the main filter. Some commentators say it comes close to criminalising lying.

Exam pitfalls
- Asking whether anyone was deceived for s2.
- Forgetting that s11 needs services actually obtained.
- Treating a moral duty as enough for s3.

notes.h: Denials of offence: automatism, insanity, intoxication and mistake
notes.body:
These pleas deny that D had the voluntary conduct or mens rea the offence requires.

Automatism
An act done without control by the mind, such as a spasm or reflex, or by someone unaware of what he is doing (Bratty v AG for NI [1963]). There must be total loss of voluntary control; impaired awareness is not enough (AG's Ref (No 2 of 1992)). Sane automatism leads to complete acquittal.

Insanity
Under the M'Naghten Rules (1843), D must suffer a defect of reason from a disease of the mind so that he did not know the nature and quality of his act or that it was wrong. D bears the burden on the balance of probabilities.
- 'Wrong' means legally wrong (R v Windle [1952]; R v Johnson [2007]).
- Internal factors are disease of the mind: epilepsy (R v Sullivan [1984]), sleepwalking (R v Burgess [1991]) and hyperglycaemia (R v Hennessy [1989]). External factors give automatism, such as hypoglycaemia caused by insulin (R v Quick [1973]). The distinction is widely criticised as arbitrary.
- Self-induced automatism (not from drink or drugs) is a defence to specific intent crimes, and to basic intent crimes unless D knew he might become aggressive or uncontrolled (R v Bailey [1983]).

Intoxication
- Voluntary intoxication can negate the mens rea of specific intent crimes (murder, s18, theft) but not basic intent crimes (manslaughter, s20, s47, reckless criminal damage) (DPP v Majewski [1977]).
- A drunken intent is still an intent, even if involuntary (R v Kingston [1995]). Dutch courage is no defence (AG for NI v Gallagher [1963]).
- Sedative drugs taken non-recklessly are treated as involuntary (R v Hardie [1985]); underestimating the strength of alcohol is not (R v Allen [1988]).

Mistake
A genuine mistaken belief in facts justifying force is judged on the facts as D believed them, reasonable or not (R v Williams (Gladstone) [1984]; Beckford v R [1988]; s76(4) CJIA 2008). A mistake caused by voluntary intoxication cannot be relied on (R v O'Grady [1987]; R v Hatton [2005]; s76(5)).

Worked example: Ian, a diabetic, takes insulin, skips food, drinks heavily and breaks Jack's jaw while confused. If hypoglycaemia caused the confusion, it is external, but self-induced; because he knew the risk, Bailey denies a defence to s20, though it may still negate the intent for s18. If alcohol caused it, Majewski applies. When Kim spikes his drink, the intoxication is involuntary, but if he still intended to smash the phone, Kingston means he has no defence.

Exam pitfalls
- Labelling diabetes cases without asking what caused the episode.
- Allowing intoxication as a defence to s20 or manslaughter.
- Forgetting that the insanity burden is on D.

Justifications mark conduct as permissible (reasonable self-defence); excuses accept the conduct was wrong but deny blame (duress). Loss of control and diminished responsibility are partial defences to murder only.

Self-defence (s76 CJIA 2008)
D is judged on the facts as he genuinely believed them, and the force must be reasonable in those circumstances. Heat-of-the-moment instinct is strong evidence of reasonableness (Palmer v R [1971]; s76(7)). In householder cases, grossly disproportionate force is never reasonable, though merely disproportionate force may be (s76(5A); R (Collins) v SSJ [2016]; R v Ray [2017]). Excessive force defeats the defence entirely (R v Clegg [1995]).

Duress
- By threats: a threat of death or serious injury to D, family or someone he reasonably feels responsible for; a genuine and reasonable belief; a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing D's characteristics would have acted the same (R v Graham [1982]); no evasive action available; and no voluntary association with criminals where coercion was foreseeable (R v Hasan [2005]).
- Not available for murder (R v Howe [1987]) or attempted murder (R v Gotts [1992]), even for a child (R v Wilson [2007]).
- Duress of circumstances follows the same test (R v Conway [1989]; R v Martin [1989]).
- Necessity is no defence to murder (R v Dudley and Stephens (1884)), but was accepted in Re A (Conjoined Twins) [2001].

Loss of control (ss54–55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009)
A loss of self-control, which need not be sudden, from a qualifying trigger (fear of serious violence, or things done or said of an extremely grave character causing a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged), where a person of D's sex and age with normal tolerance might have reacted similarly. Sexual infidelity alone is excluded but can be context (R v Clinton [2012]). Considered revenge is excluded (s54(4)).

Diminished responsibility (s2 Homicide Act 1957, as amended)
An abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition that substantially impaired D's ability to understand, form rational judgment or exercise self-control, and explains the killing. 'Substantially' means important or weighty (R v Golds [2016]). Acute intoxication alone does not qualify (R v Dowds [2012]); with a genuine abnormality, ask whether it substantially impaired D despite the drink (R v Dietschmann [2003]). D bears the burden.

Worked example: Lola, abused and threatened for years, hides a knife and stabs Max during later taunting. Self-defence is weak, as no attack was imminent. Loss of control may rest on both triggers, but the hidden knife suggests considered revenge. Diminished responsibility (PTSD, depression) is probably strongest.

Exam pitfalls
- Requiring a sudden loss of control.
- Allowing duress for murder.
- Treating excessive force as a partial defence.

cards.b: The external elements of an offence: the prohibited conduct, any required circumstances and, for result crimes, the prohibited consequence. The conduct must generally be voluntary.

The fault element in the offence definition, such as intention, recklessness, knowledge, belief or dishonesty. It is assessed element by element, so one offence may require different mental states for different parts of the actus reus.

A husband shot his wife and claimed it was an accident. The House of Lords held the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt (the 'golden thread'), subject only to insanity and statutory exceptions.
D accidentally drove onto a constable's foot, then refused to move off. Battery could be a continuing act, so the mens rea formed while the car remained there coincided with the actus reus.

Ds beat V intending to kill him, believed him dead and rolled him over a cliff; he died of exposure. Where the acts form one series or plan, it does not matter that the mens rea and the fatal act did not coincide exactly.
D swung a belt at one man and struck a woman beside him. His mens rea transferred to the actual victim because the intended and actual harm were of the same offence.
D threw a stone at people and broke a window. Malice does not transfer between offences of a different kind, so an intention to harm persons could not supply the mens rea for damaging property.

A landlady who did not know her tenants smoked cannabis was not guilty of being concerned in the management of premises used for that purpose. There is a presumption that Parliament intends mens rea for truly criminal offences.
D believed a 13-year-old girl was over 14. The House of Lords applied the presumption of mens rea to the age element: a genuine belief, reasonable or not, negated the mental element.

An offence requiring no mens rea as to at least one element of the actus reus. In Pharmaceutical Society v Storkwain [1986], pharmacists who supplied drugs on forged prescriptions were guilty although they were not at fault.

D, brought into the UK against her will by the police, was guilty as an alien 'found' in the UK. Winzar v CC of Kent (1983), where a drunk removed onto a highway by police was 'found drunk' there, is similar; both are criticised for punishing involuntary states.

The ideal that mens rea should match each element of the actus reus. Constructive offences depart from it, e.g. s47 OAPA 1861 (mens rea needed only for the assault), unlawful act manslaughter, and the GBH form of murder.
English law imposes no general duty to act, so failing to prevent harm is not criminal unless D was under a recognised duty and the offence can be committed by omission.

A railway gatekeeper left the crossing gate open and a cart driver was killed. A contractual duty can ground liability for manslaughter by omission, even towards people who are not parties to the contract.

Ds took in Stone's anorexic sister, made feeble attempts to help, and she died. By voluntarily assuming care of a helpless person they came under a duty, and their grossly negligent failure made them guilty of manslaughter.

A squatter fell asleep with a lit cigarette, woke to find the mattress smouldering and simply moved rooms. One who creates a dangerous situation and becomes aware of it must take reasonable steps to counteract it; he was guilty of arson.

D supplied heroin to her half-sister, saw the symptoms of overdose and did not summon help. Extending Miller, D owed a duty because she had contributed to a life-threatening state she knew of or ought to have known of; gross negligence manslaughter.
D put poison in his mother's drink, but she died of heart failure before it could act. He was not a 'but for' cause of death, so he was guilty only of attempted murder.

D used his pregnant girlfriend as a shield while firing at police, who shot back and killed her. D's act need only be a more than minimal cause, and the officers' reasonable self-defensive reaction did not break the chain.

Negligent treatment of a complication after a tracheotomy contributed to the death of a shooting victim. Medical treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent of D's acts, and so potent, that D's contribution becomes insignificant.
V jumped from a moving car to escape D's sexual advances. A victim's reaction breaks the chain only if it is so 'daft' or unexpected that no reasonable person could have foreseen it.

A stabbed Jehovah's Witness refused a blood transfusion and died. Under the thin skull rule D takes his victim as he finds him, including her religious beliefs, so the refusal did not break the chain.

D prepared a syringe of heroin and handed it to V, who injected himself and died. The free, deliberate and informed act of a fully informed adult breaks the chain, so D was not guilty of unlawful act manslaughter.

cards.f: R v G [2003]: test for recklessness
cards.b: D is reckless as to a circumstance or result if he is aware of a risk that it exists or will occur and, in the circumstances known to him, it is unreasonable to take that risk. The test is subjective.

cards.f: Why R v G overruled Caldwell
cards.b: Caldwell [1982] allowed liability for failing to consider an obvious risk, producing injustice in Elliott v C (1983), where a 14-year-old girl with learning difficulties could not have appreciated the risk. The Lords in G held serious crime should require a culpable state of mind and that Caldwell had misread the 1971 Act.

cards.f: Basic criminal damage: s1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971
cards.b: Without lawful excuse, destroying or damaging property belonging to another, intending to do so or being reckless as to whether it would be destroyed or damaged. Maximum 10 years (s4).

A question of fact and degree covering physical harm or impairment of value or usefulness, including temporary harm that costs time or money to put right. In Morphitis v Salmon [1990] a scratch on a scaffold bar was not damage as it did not affect its value or usefulness.

cards.f: Hardman v CC of Avon and Somerset [1986]
cards.b: Protesters painted silhouettes on a pavement in water-soluble paint, which the council paid to remove. This was damage even though rain would eventually have washed the paint away.
D stuffed a blanket down a police cell toilet and flooded the cell. The blanket and cell were damaged because they were unusable until cleaned or dried, even though the harm was temporary.
Tangible property, real or personal, including land, money and tamed or captive wild animals. Mushrooms, flowers, fruit and foliage growing wild are excluded, and intangible property is not covered.

A tenant removed wall panels he had installed, believing they were his, though in law they had become the landlord's. A genuine belief that the property is one's own, even if based on a mistake of civil law, negates the mens rea of s1(1).

Damaging any property (including one's own), intending or being reckless as to the damage, and intending or being reckless as to whether life would be endangered by that damage. Maximum life; the s5 lawful excuses do not apply.

D fired a rifle at a window behind which people stood. For s1(2) the danger to life must come from the damage itself, not from the act that caused it (the bullets), so D was not guilty of the aggravated offence.
Criminal damage under s1(1) or s1(2) committed by destroying or damaging property by fire. It is charged as arson and carries a maximum of life imprisonment.

D has a lawful excuse if he believed the person entitled to consent would have consented to the damage. By s5(3) the belief need only be honestly held; in Jaggard v Dickinson [1981] a drunken belief that the house belonged to a friend sufficed.

D damaged property to protect property he believed was in immediate need of protection, believing the means used were reasonable. The beliefs are judged subjectively, but whether D acted 'in order to protect property' is tested objectively (R v Hill and Hall (1989)).

Arising from the toppling of the Colston statue in Bristol. The Court of Appeal held that protesters who cause significant damage to property cannot rely on their Article 10 or 11 rights as a defence to criminal damage.
Intentionally or recklessly causing V to apprehend immediate unlawful force. Charged under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988; summary only, maximum 6 months.

Intentionally or recklessly applying unlawful force to another, however slight; no injury is needed. Collins v Wilcock [1984] recognises implied consent to the ordinary physical contact of everyday life.

Silent telephone calls can be an assault if they make V apprehend immediate unlawful force, and fear of force within a minute or two may count as immediate. Words alone, or even silence, can therefore constitute an assault.

An assault or battery occasioning ABH: any hurt or injury calculated to interfere with V's health or comfort that is more than transient or trifling (R v Miller [1954]; R v Donovan [1934]); a momentary loss of consciousness sufficed in T v DPP [2003]. Cutting off V's ponytail was ABH in DPP v Smith [2006]. Maximum 5 years.

cards.f: R v Savage; DPP v Parmenter [1992]
cards.b: For s47, D need only have the mens rea for the assault or battery, not foresight of ABH. For s20, D must foresee that some physical harm, not necessarily serious, might result.
Unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting GBH on another. The mens rea is intention or recklessness as to some harm (R v Mowatt [1968]); maximum 5 years.

GBH is 'really serious harm' (DPP v Smith [1961]) or simply 'serious harm' (R v Saunders [1985]), judged with regard to the victim's age and health (R v Bollom [2003]). A wound needs a break in the whole skin (JCC v Eisenhower [1984]).
A stalker caused his victim a severe depressive illness. GBH includes serious psychiatric injury, and 'inflict' in s20 does not require an assault or the direct application of force.
Unlawfully and maliciously wounding or causing GBH with intent to do GBH, or with intent to resist or prevent lawful arrest. A specific intent offence with a maximum of life imprisonment.

Consenting adult men inflicted injuries on each other in private sadomasochistic activity. The Lords held (3–2) that consent is no defence to ABH or worse unless the activity falls within a recognised public-interest exception; sadomasochism did not.

cards.f: Recognised exceptions to the Brown consent rule
cards.b: They include properly conducted sports (R v Barnes [2004]), reasonable surgery, tattooing and piercing, rough horseplay (R v Jones (1986); R v Aitken [1992]) and, per R v Wilson [1996], consensual branding between spouses. R v Emmett [1999] (asphyxiation and burns during sex) fell outside them.

cards.f: R v Dica [2004] / R v Konzani [2005]
cards.b: Recklessly transmitting HIV through sex can be s20 GBH. V's consent to the risk is a defence only if it is informed consent, which requires knowledge of D's condition.

Puts Brown on a statutory footing for sexual activity: V's consent to serious harm (ABH, wounding or GBH) for sexual gratification is no defence, except where V is infected with a sexually transmitted infection after consenting to sex knowing or believing that D had it.

Section 75A Serious Crime Act 2015, inserted by the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, criminalises intentionally strangling V or doing another act affecting V's breathing that amounts to battery. Maximum 5 years; consent is a defence unless V suffered serious harm that D intended or was reckless about.
Unlawfully killing a human being under the King's peace with malice aforethought, meaning an intention to kill or to cause GBH. It carries a mandatory life sentence.

cards.f: R v Vickers [1957] / R v Cunningham [1982]
cards.b: An intention to cause GBH is sufficient malice aforethought, even if D neither intended nor foresaw death. This 'GBH rule' is criticised as constructive liability for the most serious offence.

Direct intention: the result is D's aim or purpose. Oblique intention: the result is not D's purpose but is a virtually certain consequence that D appreciates, from which the jury may find intention (Woollin).

D shot his stepfather during a drunken contest over who could load and fire fastest. Foresight of consequences is evidence of intention, not intention itself, and intention should usually be left to the jury without elaborate direction.

D poured paraffin through a letterbox and set it alight, killing a child. The jury could not infer intention unless death or serious harm was virtually certain to result from D's actions and D appreciated that.

D threw his three-month-old son onto a hard surface, killing him. The Lords approved the Nedrick direction but replaced 'infer' with 'find': the jury is not entitled to find intention unless death or serious harm was a virtual certainty and D appreciated that.

Ds threw V, who said he could not swim, from a bridge into a river. Woollin states a rule of evidence, not substantive law: appreciation of virtual certainty permits, but does not compel, a finding of intention.

D stabbed a pregnant woman; the baby was born prematurely and died. A foetus is not a person for murder and malice cannot be transferred twice (mother to foetus to child), but unlawful act manslaughter was available.

D (1) intentionally does an unlawful act that is a crime (R v Lamb [1967]), (2) which is objectively dangerous (R v Church [1966]), and (3) which causes death. D need not foresee any harm (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977]).

cards.f: R v Dawson (1985) vs R v Watson [1989]
cards.b: For dangerousness, the reasonable bystander has the knowledge D had or would have gained during the act. In Dawson the victim's heart condition was unknown and not apparent, so the conviction was quashed; in Watson the burglar would have seen the victim's age and frailty during the burglary.

cards.f: Gross negligence manslaughter: R v Adomako [1995]
cards.b: An anaesthetist failed to notice a disconnected oxygen tube. D is guilty if he owed a duty of care, breached it, the breach caused death, and the negligence was so bad that the jury considers it criminal.

An optometrist failed to examine the back of a child's eye and missed a fatal condition. The serious and obvious risk of death must be reasonably foreseeable at the time of breach on the information then available, not on what a proper examination would have revealed.
Dishonestly appropriating property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it. Maximum 7 years (s7).

cards.f: Appropriation: s3(1) and R v Morris [1984]
cards.b: Any assumption of the rights of an owner. Morris (switching price labels in a supermarket) held that assuming any one of the owner's rights is enough.

D induced his manager to accept worthless cheques for goods. Following Lawrence v MPC [1972], an act may be an appropriation even though the owner consented to or authorised it, including consent obtained by deception.

D received about £60,000 and a television as 'gifts' from a man of limited intelligence. Receiving a valid gift that passes indefeasible title can still be an appropriation; dishonesty separates guilty from innocent conduct.
A student read an examination paper before the exam and returned it. Confidential information is not 'property' under s4, so there was no theft.
D took his own car from a garage that had repaired it, without paying. Property 'belongs to' anyone in possession or control of it (s5(1)), so an owner can steal his own property.

s5(3): property received under an obligation to deal with it in a particular way is treated as belonging to the transferor (R v Hall [1973]: travel agent's deposits; no such obligation proved). s5(4): property got by another's mistake, under an obligation to restore it, belongs to the person entitled (AG's Ref (No 1 of 1983): overpaid wages).

D is not dishonest if he appropriates believing (a) he has a legal right to deprive the other, (b) the other would consent if he knew, or (c) the owner cannot be discovered by taking reasonable steps. Under s2(2), willingness to pay does not prevent dishonesty.

cards.f: Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] / R v Barton and Booth [2020]
cards.b: The tribunal first finds D's actual knowledge or belief as to the facts (genuineness, not reasonableness, matters), then asks whether his conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. Barton and Booth confirmed this replaces the subjective second limb of R v Ghosh [1982] in criminal cases.

A cinema projectionist lent films for copying and returned them within hours. Under s6, borrowing amounts to an intention to permanently deprive only if the thing is returned with all its goodness or virtue gone; the films were unaffected.

Stealing and, immediately before or at the time and in order to steal, using force on any person or putting or seeking to put any person in fear of force. Slight force can suffice (R v Dawson and James (1976); R v Clouden [1987]). Maximum life.

cards.f: R v Hale (1978) / R v Robinson [1977]
cards.b: Hale: appropriation is a continuing act, so force used in tying up V after the jewellery was taken was 'at the time of' stealing. Robinson: a genuine belief in a legal right to the money negated dishonesty, so there was no theft and therefore no robbery.

s9(1)(a): entering a building as a trespasser intending to steal, inflict GBH or do unlawful damage; s9(1)(b): having entered as a trespasser, stealing or inflicting GBH, or attempting to. Entry must be 'effective' (R v Brown [1985]); in R v Ryan (1996) a man stuck with his head and arm through a window had entered.
One offence committable in three ways: false representation (s2), failing to disclose information (s3) and abuse of position (s4). Maximum 10 years.

Dishonestly making a false representation, intending by it to make a gain or to cause loss or expose another to a risk of loss. A representation is false if untrue or misleading and D knows it is, or might be, untrue or misleading.

Any representation of fact or law, including about the state of mind of D or another; it may be express or implied, for example by conduct. It can be made to a machine or system designed to respond without human intervention.

cards.f: Implied representations: MPC v Charles [1977] / R v Lambie [1982]
cards.b: Using a cheque card or credit card impliedly represents that D has the bank's authority to use it. These pre-2006 deception cases remain useful for identifying implied representations under s2.

D ordered a meal intending to pay, changed his mind and ran out. By remaining seated he made a continuing implied representation that he intended to pay, which became false when his intention changed.

Under the 2006 Act no one need be deceived, nothing need be obtained and no gain or loss need actually occur: the offence is complete when the false representation is made with the required dishonesty and intent.
Gain and loss extend only to money or other property, whether temporary or permanent. Gain includes keeping what one has; loss includes not getting what one might get.

cards.f: Fraud by failing to disclose: s3
cards.b: Dishonestly failing to disclose information that D is under a legal duty to disclose, intending to make a gain or cause loss. The duty may arise from statute, contract, a fiduciary relationship or trade custom, but a merely moral duty is not enough.

cards.f: Fraud by abuse of position: s4 and R v Valujevs [2014]
cards.b: D occupies a position in which he is expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests and dishonestly abuses it, possibly by omission. Valujevs held the position is not confined to fiduciary relationships; gangmasters controlling workers' pay could occupy one.

cards.f: Obtaining services dishonestly: s11 Fraud Act 2006
cards.b: Obtaining, by a dishonest act, services made available on the basis of payment, without paying in full, knowing payment is required. Unlike s2 it is a result crime: the services must actually be obtained. Maximum 5 years.

cards.f: Articles for use in fraud: ss6–7 Fraud Act 2006
cards.b: s6 criminalises possessing or controlling any article for use in the course of or in connection with fraud; s7 criminalises making, adapting, supplying or offering to supply such articles.

cards.f: Main criticism of the Fraud Act 2006
cards.b: Removing any need for deception, obtaining or loss moves liability to a very early stage and makes the jury's view of dishonesty the main filter, leading commentators to argue that the Act comes close to criminalising lying.

cards.f: Automatism: Bratty v AG for Northern Ireland [1963]
cards.b: An act done by the muscles without any control by the mind, such as a spasm or reflex, or an act done by a person not conscious of what he is doing. Sane automatism leads to a complete acquittal.

cards.f: Total loss of control: AG's Reference (No 2 of 1992) [1994]
cards.b: A lorry driver 'driving without awareness' after long hours crashed, killing two people. Automatism requires total destruction of voluntary control; reduced or impaired awareness is not enough.

A malfunction caused by an external factor (e.g. a blow or an injection) is sane automatism; one caused by an internal factor, a disease of the mind, is insanity. R v Quick [1973] (hypoglycaemia from insulin) was automatism; R v Hennessy [1989] (hyperglycaemia from the diabetes itself) was insanity.

cards.f: R v Sullivan [1984] and R v Burgess [1991]
cards.b: Sullivan: an assault during an epileptic seizure fell within insanity, as 'disease of the mind' covers any internal impairment of mental faculties, organic or functional, permanent or transient. Burgess: violent sleepwalking also stemmed from an internal factor and so was insanity.

D is legally insane if at the time of the act he was labouring under such a defect of reason, from disease of the mind, as not to know the nature and quality of his act or, if he did, not to know it was wrong. D bears the burden on the balance of probabilities.

cards.f: R v Windle [1952] / R v Johnson [2007]
cards.b: 'Wrong' in the M'Naghten Rules means legally wrong. A defendant who knows his act is against the law cannot plead insanity even if he believes it morally justified.

A diabetic failed to eat after taking insulin and struck V with an iron bar. Self-induced automatism not caused by drink or drugs is a defence to specific intent crimes, and to basic intent crimes unless D knew his conduct could make him aggressive, unpredictable or uncontrolled.

Voluntary intoxication can be used to show D lacked the mens rea of a specific intent offence (e.g. murder, s18, theft), but not a basic intent offence (e.g. manslaughter, s20, s47, reckless criminal damage), because becoming intoxicated supplies the fault.

cards.f: A drunken intent is still an intent: R v Kingston [1995]
cards.b: D, secretly drugged by another, indecently assaulted a boy. Because he still formed the intent, involuntary intoxication was no defence: intoxication matters only if D actually lacked the mens rea.

cards.f: AG for Northern Ireland v Gallagher [1963]
cards.b: D decided to kill his wife, bought a knife and whisky, drank for 'Dutch courage', then killed her. Intoxication is no defence where D forms the intent while sober and drinks to carry it out.

cards.f: R v Hardie [1985] vs R v Allen [1988]
cards.b: Hardie took old Valium to calm himself and then started a fire: taking a drug generally known to be sedative is treated like involuntary intoxication unless D was reckless in taking it. Allen did not realise how strong his wine was: that was still voluntary intoxication.

D, mistakenly believing V was assaulting a youth, intervened with force. A genuine mistaken belief in facts that would justify force is assessed on the facts as D believed them, even if the belief was unreasonable; confirmed in Beckford v R [1988] and s76(4) CJIA 2008.

cards.f: Intoxicated mistake: R v O'Grady [1987] / R v Hatton [2005]
cards.b: D cannot rely on a mistaken belief in the need to use force in self-defence that was caused by voluntary intoxication, even on a murder charge. Section 76(5) CJIA 2008 now states this.

A justification marks conduct as permissible in the circumstances (e.g. reasonable self-defence); an excuse accepts the conduct was wrong but holds D not blameworthy because of pressure or incapacity (e.g. duress).

cards.f: Self-defence: s76 Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008
cards.b: D is judged on the facts as he genuinely believed them, and the force must be reasonable in those circumstances. Doing what one honestly and instinctively thought necessary in the heat of the moment is strong evidence of reasonableness (s76(7); Palmer v R [1971]).

Where a householder uses force against an intruder in a dwelling, force is unreasonable if grossly disproportionate. R (Collins) v SSJ [2016] and R v Ray [2017] held that disproportionate force may still be reasonable, but grossly disproportionate force never is.

A soldier fired the fatal shot after the car had passed his checkpoint and the danger was over. Excessive force means self-defence fails completely; there is no partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter for excessive force as such.

cards.f: Duress by threats: R v Hasan [2005]
cards.b: Requires a threat of death or serious injury to D, his family or someone for whom he reasonably feels responsible; a genuine and reasonable belief in the threat; that a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing D's characteristics would have done the same (R v Graham [1982]); no evasive action reasonably open; and no voluntary association with criminals where D foresaw or ought to have foreseen the risk of compulsion.

cards.f: Limits of duress: R v Howe [1987] and R v Gotts [1992]
cards.b: Duress is no defence to murder, as principal or secondary party (Howe), or to attempted murder (Gotts). R v Wilson [2007] applied this even to a 13-year-old acting under his father's threats.

cards.f: Duress of circumstances: R v Conway [1989] / R v Martin [1989]
cards.b: Duress can arise from circumstances rather than a demand to commit a crime. Conway drove recklessly to escape men he believed would kill his passenger; Martin drove while disqualified because his wife threatened suicide. The Graham test applies.
Shipwrecked sailors killed and ate the cabin boy to survive. Necessity is no defence to murder.

Separation surgery would save Jodie but inevitably kill Mary. The Court of Appeal held it lawful; Brooke LJ relied on necessity: the act must be needed to avoid inevitable and irreparable evil, go no further than reasonably necessary, and not be disproportionate to the evil avoided.

cards.f: Loss of control: s54 Coroners and Justice Act 2009
cards.b: A partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter. D's acts must result from a loss of self-control (which need not be sudden) with a qualifying trigger, and a person of D's sex and age with normal tolerance and self-restraint, in D's circumstances, might have reacted in the same or a similar way.

(1) Fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person; (2) things done or said that constitute circumstances of an extremely grave character and cause D a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged; or both. A trigger D incited as an excuse to use violence is disregarded.

cards.f: Sexual infidelity and revenge: R v Clinton [2012]
cards.b: Section 55(6)(c) excludes sexual infidelity as a trigger on its own, but Clinton held it may be considered as context where another trigger is present. Section 54(4) excludes the defence where D acted in a considered desire for revenge.

cards.f: Diminished responsibility: s2 Homicide Act 1957 (as amended by s52 CJA 2009)
cards.b: An abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition that substantially impaired D's ability to understand his conduct, form a rational judgment or exercise self-control, and that provides an explanation for the killing (a significant contributory factor). D must prove it on the balance of probabilities.

The Supreme Court held that 'substantially' in s2 Homicide Act 1957 means an 'important or weighty' impairment, not merely one that is more than trivial. Judges should not normally define the word for the jury unless there is a risk of misunderstanding.

cards.f: R v Dowds [2012] / R v Dietschmann [2003]
cards.b: Acute voluntary intoxication is not a 'recognised medical condition' for diminished responsibility (Dowds). Where D was intoxicated and also had a genuine abnormality, the jury asks whether the abnormality substantially impaired him despite the drink (Dietschmann).

questions.q: Which case established that the prosecution bears the burden of proving the defendant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, subject to insanity and statutory exceptions?
options: R v Woollin [1999]
Woolmington v DPP [1935]
Sweet v Parsley [1970]
R v Miller [1983]
questions.why: Woolmington set out the 'golden thread' that the prosecution must prove guilt. The other cases deal with oblique intention, the presumption of mens rea and liability for omissions.

questions.q: Dan throws a brick at Eve, intending to hit her. He misses and the brick smashes a shop window. Which statement best describes Dan's liability for criminal damage to the window?
options: He is guilty because his intention to hit Eve transfers to the window under the doctrine of transferred malice
He cannot be guilty of criminal damage because he intended to harm a person, not property
His intention cannot transfer from a person to property, but he is guilty if he was aware of a risk of damaging the window and it was unreasonable to take it
He is guilty because criminal damage is an offence of strict liability as to the ownership of the property
questions.why: R v Pembliton (1874) shows malice does not transfer between different kinds of offence. Dan may still be guilty of criminal damage on his own recklessness under R v G [2003].

questions.q: Distinguish between a conduct crime and a result crime, giving one example of each.
markScheme: A conduct crime is complete once the prohibited conduct takes place, whatever its consequences; e.g. fraud by false representation or perjury
A result crime requires the conduct to cause a prohibited consequence, so causation must be proved; e.g. murder or criminal damage
questions.modelAnswer: A conduct crime is defined only by D's behaviour, perhaps in certain circumstances, and needs no particular outcome. Fraud by false representation under s2 Fraud Act 2006 is an example: the offence is complete when the false representation is made, whether or not anyone is deceived. A result crime needs the conduct to bring about a specified consequence, so the prosecution must prove causation. Murder, which requires D to cause death, is an example, as is criminal damage.

questions.q: Explain the presumption of mens rea and the circumstances in which the courts will treat a statutory offence as one of strict liability.
markScheme: Where a statute is silent, courts presume Parliament intended mens rea to be required (Sweet v Parsley [1970]; B v DPP [2000])
The presumption is displaced only clearly or by necessary implication from the statute's words and context
Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v AG of Hong Kong [1985]: the presumption is particularly strong for truly criminal offences and is weaker for regulatory offences dealing with public safety or social concern
Strict liability should be imposed only if it will effectively promote the statute's objects by encouraging greater vigilance; severity of penalty and stigma point against it
questions.modelAnswer: Where a statutory offence does not mention mens rea, the courts presume that Parliament meant a mental element to be required (Sweet v Parsley [1970]), and in B v DPP [2000] this presumption was applied to the age element of an offence. It can be displaced only expressly or by necessary implication. Gammon v AG of Hong Kong [1985] sets out the guiding factors. The presumption is strongest for 'truly criminal' offences that carry stigma and heavy penalties. It is weaker for regulatory offences on matters of social concern such as public safety, food or pollution. Even then, strict liability should be imposed only where it would actually promote the statute's purpose by encouraging people to take greater care.

questions.q: According to R v G [2003], a person acts recklessly as to a result when:
options: the risk of the result would have been obvious to a reasonable person, whether or not D considered it
D is aware of a risk that the result will occur and, in the circumstances known to him, it is unreasonable to take that risk
D foresees the result as a virtual certainty
D fails to take the care that a reasonable person would have taken
questions.why: R v G restored the subjective test: D must actually be aware of the risk, and taking it must be unreasonable. The 'obvious to a reasonable person whether or not D considered it' test is the overruled Caldwell test, and failing to take reasonable care describes negligence.

questions.q: In which situation is the chain of causation most likely to be broken, so that D is not liable for V's death?
options: V, stabbed by D, refuses a blood transfusion on religious grounds and dies
V, shot by D, dies after hospital doctors negligently fail to spot a complication of the treatment for the wound
D prepares a syringe of heroin and hands it to V, a fully informed adult, who injects himself and dies
D uses V as a human shield while shooting at police, who return fire and kill V
questions.why: R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] holds that the free, deliberate and informed act of an adult breaks the chain. The others reflect Blaue, Cheshire and Pagett, where the chain was not broken.

questions.q: Identify three situations in which English criminal law recognises a duty to act, citing an authority for each.
markScheme: Contractual duty, e.g. R v Pittwood (1902)
Voluntary assumption of care for a helpless person, e.g. R v Stone and Dobinson [1977] or R v Instan [1893]

Creating a dangerous situation, e.g. R v Miller [1983] or R v Evans [2009]; also accept a special relationship such as parent and child (R v Gibbins and Proctor (1918)), public office (R v Dytham [1979]) or a statutory duty
questions.modelAnswer: English law has no general duty to act, but duties arise in recognised categories. A contract can create one: in R v Pittwood (1902) a gatekeeper who left a level crossing open was liable for a resulting death. A duty also arises where D voluntarily takes on the care of someone unable to look after themselves (R v Stone and Dobinson [1977]). Under R v Miller [1983], someone who creates a dangerous situation and becomes aware of it must take reasonable steps to deal with it, and R v Evans [2009] extended this to contributing to a drug overdose. Special relationships such as parent and child (Gibbins and Proctor) also create duties.

questions.q: Using Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993], explain why a doctor who withdraws life-sustaining treatment from a patient in a permanent vegetative state is not guilty of murder, and identify one criticism of the reasoning.
markScheme: The House of Lords classified withdrawal of treatment (including artificial feeding) as an omission rather than a positive act
An omission is criminal only if D is under a duty to act; a doctor's duty is to provide treatment that is in the patient's best interests
Continuing futile treatment for a patient with no prospect of recovery was not in his best interests, so there was no duty to continue and no breach
Criticism: the act/omission line is artificial here (switching off a machine looks like an act, and an outsider doing it would be guilty), and the outcome turns on labels rather than moral substance
questions.modelAnswer: In Bland the House of Lords treated withdrawing artificial feeding from Tony Bland as an omission, not an act. An omission is criminal only where there is a duty to act, and a doctor's duty is to give treatment that is in the patient's best interests. Bland had no prospect of recovery, so continuing invasive treatment was not in his best interests; the doctors had no duty to continue it and withdrawing it was lawful. Critics call this artificial. Switching off a machine looks like an act, and an intruder doing the same would commit murder, so the outcome seems to turn on labels rather than the real moral question.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT 'property' for the purposes of the Criminal Damage Act 1971?
options: A rented flat
Mushrooms growing wild on common land
A pet rabbit
A bank's cash stored in its vault
questions.why: Section 10(1) excludes mushrooms, flowers, fruit and foliage growing wild. Land, tamed animals and money are all tangible property within the Act.

questions.q: Fay fires an air rifle at a café window, shattering it. Customers sitting just behind the glass are showered with fragments but unhurt. Fay foresaw that people might be hit by her pellets. On a charge of aggravated criminal damage under s1(2) CDA 1971, which is correct?
options: She is guilty because she was reckless as to endangering life by firing the rifle
She is not guilty because no one was actually injured
She is guilty only if she was reckless as to life being endangered by the damage to the window itself, such as flying glass
She is not guilty because s1(2) requires the property to belong to another
questions.why: Under R v Steer [1988], the danger to life must come from the damage, not from the missile that caused it. Actual endangerment is unnecessary, and s1(2) covers any property, including D's own.

questions.q: Explain the lawful excuse defences in s5 Criminal Damage Act 1971 and how the courts have limited them.
markScheme: s5(2)(a): belief that the person entitled to consent had consented or would have consented to the damage
s5(2)(b): damage to protect property believed to be in immediate need of protection by means believed reasonable
s5(3): it is immaterial whether the belief is justified, if honestly held; a drunken belief sufficed in Jaggard v Dickinson [1981]
Limits: whether D acted 'in order to protect' property is tested objectively (R v Hill and Hall (1989)); God is not a person entitled to consent (Blake v DPP [1993]); s5 does not apply to s1(2)
questions.modelAnswer: Section 5(2)(a) gives a lawful excuse where D believed the person entitled to consent had consented, or would have consented, to the damage. Section 5(2)(b) covers damage done to protect property D believed was in immediate need of protection, by means D believed reasonable. By s5(3) these beliefs need only be honest, so a drunken mistake sufficed in Jaggard v Dickinson [1981]. The courts have limited the defences. R v Hill and Hall (1989) held that whether D acted 'in order to protect property' is objective. Blake v DPP [1993] held that God is not a person entitled to consent. Neither defence applies to aggravated criminal damage.

questions.q: In the Offences Against the Person Act 1861, 'grievous bodily harm' has been held to mean:
options: Any hurt or injury calculated to interfere with health or comfort
Really serious harm, or simply serious harm
Harm that is more than transient or trifling
Any break in the continuity of the whole skin
questions.why: DPP v Smith [1961] and R v Saunders [1985] define GBH as really serious or serious harm. Hurt calculated to interfere with health or comfort, and harm more than transient or trifling, describe ABH; a break in the continuity of the whole skin describes a wound.

questions.q: Gus pushes Hal, intending only to shove him out of the way. Hal falls awkwardly and fractures his wrist. Gus did not foresee any injury. Which offence is Gus most likely to have committed?
options: Battery only, because he did not foresee any harm
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm under s47 OAPA 1861
Inflicting grievous bodily harm under s20 OAPA 1861
Causing grievous bodily harm with intent under s18 OAPA 1861
questions.why: Under R v Savage; DPP v Parmenter [1992], s47 needs only the mens rea of the battery, not foresight of harm. Section 20 would need foresight of some harm, and s18 an intention to cause serious harm.

questions.q: Distinguish the offences in s20 and s18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.
markScheme: Both cover wounding or GBH; s20 uses 'inflict' and s18 uses 'cause', though after R v Burstow [1998] there is little practical difference
s20 mens rea: intention or recklessness as to some harm (R v Mowatt [1968]; Parmenter); maximum 5 years
s18 mens rea: specific intent to do GBH (or to resist or prevent arrest); maximum life; a specific intent offence for the purposes of voluntary intoxication
questions.modelAnswer: Both offences cover wounding or GBH. Section 20 speaks of 'inflicting' GBH and s18 of 'causing' it, though Burstow [1998] has largely removed any difference between the two words. The key distinction is mens rea. For s20, D need only intend or foresee that some physical harm, not necessarily serious, might result (Mowatt; Parmenter). Section 18 needs an intention to cause GBH, or to resist or prevent lawful arrest. That is why s18 carries a maximum of life imprisonment while s20 carries five years, and why voluntary intoxication can negate the mens rea of s18 but not of s20.

questions.q: Outline the reasoning of the majority in R v Brown [1994] and explain how R v Wilson [1996] was distinguished.
markScheme: The majority held that consent is no defence to ABH or more serious harm unless the activity falls within a recognised category of public interest
Reasons included public policy: risk of serious injury and infection, the potential to corrupt young men, and 'the cult of violence'

Lord Templeman framed the question as whether there was good reason to add sadomasochism to the exceptions; the minority (Lords Mustill and Slynn) saw it as private conduct the criminal law should not reach

Wilson: a husband branded initials on his wife's buttocks at her request; it was compared to tattooing, a matter of personal adornment between spouses with no aggressive intent, so consent was a defence
questions.modelAnswer: The Brown majority held that consent is no defence where ABH or worse is caused, unless the activity falls within a recognised public-interest exception such as sport or surgery. They refused to create a new exception for sadomasochism, pointing to the risks of escalating injury and infection and the corruption of young men. Lords Mustill and Slynn dissented, regarding the conduct as private. In R v Wilson [1996] a husband branded his initials on his wife's buttocks at her request. The Court of Appeal likened this to tattooing, personal adornment between spouses with no aggressive intent, and held consent was a defence.

questions.q: Under R v Woollin [1999], a jury is not entitled to find that D intended to kill or cause serious harm unless:
options: death or serious harm was a highly probable consequence of D's act
death or serious harm was a virtual certainty as a result of D's actions, and D appreciated that this was the case
a reasonable person would have foreseen death or serious harm as virtually certain
D desired death or serious harm as his ultimate aim
questions.why: Woollin requires both an objective virtual certainty and D's appreciation of it. Foresight of high probability (Hyam v DPP [1975]) no longer suffices after Moloney and Woollin; Hancock and Shankland treated probability only as evidence. A reasonable-person test would make intention objective.

questions.q: During a burglary of a house, Ian throws a brick at a garage window. Unknown to Ian, and not apparent from anything he saw or heard, the elderly owner has a severe heart condition. The owner hears the noise, suffers a heart attack and dies. On a charge of unlawful act manslaughter, the strongest argument for Ian is that:
options: he did not foresee any risk of harm to anyone
throwing the brick was not a criminal act
a sober and reasonable person with Ian's knowledge would not have recognised a risk of some physical harm to anyone from the act
the owner's heart condition broke the chain of causation
questions.why: Dangerousness under R v Church is objective, but the bystander has only the knowledge D had or would have gained (R v Dawson (1985)). Foresight is not required (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977]), and the thin skull rule means the heart condition does not break the chain.

questions.q: State the elements of unlawful act manslaughter, citing an authority for each.
markScheme: An intentional act that is unlawful in the sense of being a criminal offence, with its full mens rea (R v Lamb [1967]); an omission will not do (R v Lowe [1973])

The act must be dangerous: one that all sober and reasonable people would recognise as carrying a risk of some physical harm (R v Church [1966]); D need not recognise it (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977])
The unlawful act must cause death, applying ordinary causation rules (e.g. R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007])
questions.modelAnswer: Unlawful act manslaughter needs, first, a deliberate act that is a criminal offence, with all of that offence's actus reus and mens rea. In R v Lamb [1967] there was no assault because the victim did not apprehend force and Lamb had no mens rea, so there was no unlawful act. Second, the act must be objectively dangerous: sober and reasonable people would recognise that it carried a risk of some physical harm (R v Church [1966]), whether or not D did (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977]). Third, the act must cause death. Normal causation rules apply, so the free and informed self-injection in R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] broke the chain.

questions.q: Is foresight of virtual certainty intention itself, or only evidence from which intention may be found? Discuss with reference to Woollin and later authority.
markScheme: Moloney [1985] and Hancock and Shankland [1986]: foresight of consequences is evidence of intention, not intention itself
Woollin [1999] replaced 'infer' with 'find', which some commentators read as turning the test into a definition of intention
R v Matthews and Alleyne [2003]: Woollin is a rule of evidence; appreciation of virtual certainty allows but does not compel a finding of intention
This leaves the jury a residual discretion (a 'moral elbow-room'), which promotes flexibility but risks inconsistency between similar cases
Evaluation: e.g. the Law Commission (Law Com No 304, 2006) favoured codifying the Woollin approach as the basis on which intention may be found
questions.modelAnswer: Moloney [1985] and Hancock and Shankland [1986] treated foresight as evidence of intention only. Woollin replaced 'infer' with 'find', which some read as turning the test into a definition. R v Matthews and Alleyne [2003] held, however, that Woollin is a rule of evidence: once D appreciated virtual certainty, the jury may find intention but need not. This leaves the jury an undefined discretion that can soften harsh outcomes, for example in medical cases, but at the cost of certainty, since two defendants with identical foresight may be treated differently. The Law Commission (Law Com No 304) favoured keeping, and codifying, the evidential approach.

questions.q: In Oxford v Moss (1978), a student who read an examination paper in advance and returned it was not guilty of theft because:
options: he did not appropriate the paper
confidential information is not 'property' under s4 Theft Act 1968
he was not dishonest
the university had consented
questions.why: The court held that information is not property capable of being stolen. He also lacked any intention to permanently deprive the university of the paper itself.

questions.q: Jo, a carer, persuades Kay, an elderly woman of limited understanding but legally capable of making a gift, to give her £10,000. The gift is valid in civil law. Which statement reflects R v Hinks [2001]?
options: Jo cannot have appropriated the money because Kay consented
Jo cannot be guilty because ownership passed to her, so the money no longer belonged to another
Acceptance of a valid gift can be an appropriation, and Jo may be guilty of theft if her conduct is found to be dishonest
Jo can be guilty only of fraud, not theft
questions.why: Hinks held that receiving a valid gift can still be an appropriation; dishonesty is what separates criminal from innocent receipt. The property belonged to Kay at the moment of appropriation.

questions.q: Explain the test for dishonesty in theft after Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] and R v Barton and Booth [2020], including the role of s2 Theft Act 1968.
markScheme: First consider s2(1): D is not dishonest if he believed he had a legal right, that the owner would consent, or that the owner could not be found by reasonable steps
Otherwise, the tribunal first ascertains D's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts; the question is whether the belief was genuine, not whether it was reasonable
It then decides whether D's conduct was dishonest by the objective standards of ordinary decent people
D need not appreciate that his conduct was dishonest by those standards; Barton and Booth confirmed that the second limb of R v Ghosh [1982] no longer applies
questions.modelAnswer: First apply s2(1) Theft Act 1968: D is not dishonest if he believed he had a legal right to the property, that the owner would consent, or that the owner could not be found by reasonable steps. Otherwise, under Ivey, the jury finds what D actually knew or believed about the facts; reasonableness matters only as evidence of whether the belief was genuine. It then asks whether, given that state of mind, the conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. Barton and Booth [2020] confirmed that this replaces Ghosh, so D need not realise that others would regard the conduct as dishonest.

questions.q: Lia's employer mistakenly pays her £500 too much in her monthly salary. She notices, says nothing and spends it. Explain whether she could be guilty of theft.
markScheme: Issue: once credited, the money (a credit balance) is Lia's, so prima facie it does not belong to another
s5(4): where D gets property by another's mistake and is under a legal obligation to make restoration, it is treated as belonging to the person entitled to restoration
AG's Reference (No 1 of 1983) [1985]: overpaid wages fell within s5(4); a restitutionary obligation suffices
Lia appropriated by spending it, with the intention not to restore treated as an intention to permanently deprive (s5(4)); liability depends on dishonesty under s2 and Ivey
questions.modelAnswer: The difficulty is that the overpayment becomes a credit balance in Lia's own account, so at first sight it no longer belongs to another. Section 5(4) Theft Act 1968 solves this. Where property is obtained by another's mistake and D is legally obliged to restore it, it is treated as belonging to the person entitled to restoration, and an intention not to restore counts as an intention to permanently deprive. AG's Reference (No 1 of 1983) applied this to overpaid wages. Lia appropriates by spending the money. If a jury applying Ivey finds that ordinary decent people would regard keeping a known overpayment as dishonest, and none of the s2(1) beliefs applies, she is guilty of theft.

questions.q: Which statement about fraud by false representation under s2 Fraud Act 2006 is correct?
options: The representation must deceive someone and cause them to hand over property
The offence is complete when D dishonestly makes a false representation intending to make a gain or cause loss, whether or not anyone is deceived
A representation cannot be made to a machine
'Gain' and 'loss' include services and confidential information
questions.why: Section 2 is a conduct crime, and s2(5) covers representations made to machines. Section 5 confines gain and loss to money or other property.

questions.q: Identify the three ways in which fraud can be committed under s1 Fraud Act 2006 and state the core conduct element of each.
markScheme: s2 false representation: making a representation that is untrue or misleading, knowing it is or might be
s3 failing to disclose information: failing to disclose information D is under a legal duty to disclose

s4 abuse of position: abusing a position in which D is expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests (which may be by omission); all require dishonesty and intent to gain or cause loss
questions.modelAnswer: Section 1 creates a single offence of fraud that can be committed in three ways. Under s2, D makes a false representation, meaning one that is untrue or misleading, knowing that it is or might be. Under s3, D fails to disclose information that he is under a legal duty to disclose. Under s4, D abuses a position in which he is expected to safeguard, or not to act against, another person's financial interests; the abuse can be an omission. In every form D must act dishonestly and intend to make a gain or to cause loss, or expose another to the risk of loss.

questions.q: Mo orders a meal at a restaurant, intending to pay. After eating he realises he has left his wallet at home and slips out without paying. Ned orders a meal intending from the start not to pay, eats it and leaves. Compare their liability under the Fraud Act 2006.
markScheme: Ned: by ordering he impliedly represents an intention to pay (DPP v Ray [1974]); this is false and dishonest, so s2 fraud is committed when he orders
Ned also obtains services (the meal service) by a dishonest act without paying, knowing payment is required: s11 (a result crime, the service must be obtained)

Mo: no false representation when ordering because he then intended to pay; on Ray, a continuing representation may become false if he changes his mind while staying, but here leaving without paying after discovering he cannot pay is more naturally making off without payment (s3 Theft Act 1978)
Both require dishonesty under Ivey; Mo's honest intention at ordering and conduct after discovery go to whether ordinary decent people would see him as dishonest
questions.modelAnswer: Ned impliedly represents, when he orders, that he intends to pay (DPP v Ray [1974]). The representation is false and he knows it, so s2 fraud is complete when he orders, if he is dishonest under Ivey. Since he then obtains the meal without paying, he also commits s11 (obtaining services dishonestly). Mo intended to pay when ordering, so his representation was true and he obtained the meal honestly. Ray suggests a continuing representation can become false, but Mo simply discovers he cannot pay. Slipping out is better charged as making off without payment under s3 Theft Act 1978, if he intended to avoid payment permanently and was dishonest.

questions.q: An insulin-dependent diabetic attacks someone while in a confused state. In which case would the courts treat this as insanity rather than sane automatism?
options: The confusion resulted from hypoglycaemia after taking insulin and not eating
The confusion resulted from hyperglycaemia because he had not taken his insulin
The confusion resulted from a blow to the head in a car accident
The confusion resulted from a drug secretly put in his drink
questions.why: Under R v Hennessy [1989], hyperglycaemia caused by the diabetes itself is an internal factor, so the case is one of insanity. Hypoglycaemia caused by insulin is external (R v Quick [1973]), as are a blow or a spiked drink.

questions.q: Explain the rule in DPP v Majewski [1977] and give two examples each of specific and basic intent offences.
markScheme: Voluntary intoxication can be relied on to show D did not form the mens rea of a specific intent offence
It cannot be relied on for a basic intent offence; recklessness in becoming intoxicated supplies the fault
Specific intent examples: murder, s18 OAPA 1861, theft, robbery (accept burglary with intent)
Basic intent examples: manslaughter, s20, s47, assault/battery, reckless criminal damage
