questions.modelAnswer: Majewski holds that a voluntarily intoxicated defendant may use evidence of intoxication to show that he did not form the mens rea of a specific intent offence, such as murder, s18 OAPA 1861 or theft. A drunken intent is still an intent, though, so this helps only if no intent was actually formed. For basic intent offences, such as manslaughter, s20 or s47 OAPA 1861, battery and reckless criminal damage, intoxication is no answer. The House of Lords reasoned that choosing to become intoxicated is itself reckless conduct that supplies the fault for these offences. The rule is a policy compromise rather than a principled application of subjective mens rea.

questions.q: Why is the internal/external factor test for distinguishing insanity from automatism widely criticised?
markScheme: It produces arbitrary distinctions: hypoglycaemia (Quick) is automatism while hyperglycaemia (Hennessy) is insanity, though both are diabetic episodes
It labels people with epilepsy (Sullivan), diabetes and sleep disorders (Burgess) as 'insane', a stigmatising legal label far from medical understanding
Its policy basis is social protection from recurrent danger, but the test does not track dangerousness or likelihood of recurrence
It can deter defendants from raising the defence, leading to guilty pleas (as in Sullivan and Hennessy); though disposals are now flexible under the 1964 Act as amended, the label remains
questions.modelAnswer: The test produces arbitrary results. A diabetic who is hypoglycaemic after taking insulin may be acquitted outright (Quick), while one who is hyperglycaemic for failing to take it is 'insane' (Hennessy), although the medical problems are closely linked. The test classifies epilepsy (Sullivan) and sleepwalking (Burgess) as diseases of the mind, which stigmatises defendants and bears no relation to psychiatric understanding. Its supposed aim is to protect the public from recurring danger, but internal origin does not reliably predict dangerousness or recurrence. Finally, defendants faced with an insanity label have pleaded guilty instead, as Sullivan and Hennessy did. Disposals have become flexible, but the label still discourages people from raising the defence.

questions.q: Which statement about duress is correct under current English law?
options: Duress is a defence to all offences, including murder
Duress is not a defence to murder or attempted murder
Duress is a partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter
Duress is available to murder only for secondary parties
questions.why: R v Howe [1987] excludes murder, whether D is principal or secondary party, and R v Gotts [1992] excludes attempted murder. There is no partial defence of duress.

questions.q: Ola kills her husband shortly after discovering he has been having an affair. She lost her self-control on finding out, and there is no other relevant circumstance. On a plea of loss of control under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, which is correct?
options: The defence fails automatically because the loss of control was not sudden
The infidelity can found a qualifying trigger because it is a circumstance of an extremely grave character
The defence is unavailable because sexual infidelity must be disregarded as a qualifying trigger, and there is no other trigger
The infidelity can be considered because it caused a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged
questions.why: Section 55(6)(c) requires sexual infidelity to be disregarded. R v Clinton [2012] allows it to be considered only as context for another trigger, and there is none here. Suddenness is not required (s54(2)).

questions.q: Explain the 'voluntary association' limitation on duress after R v Hasan [2005] and the reasoning behind it.
markScheme: Duress is unavailable where D voluntarily associated with criminals or a criminal enterprise
Hasan: the test is whether D foresaw, or ought reasonably to have foreseen, the risk of being subjected to any compulsion by threats of violence
It is not necessary that D foresaw compulsion to commit the kind of offence actually committed (disapproving the narrower view in R v Baker and Ward [1999])
Rationale: D who chooses to join violent criminals is at fault for exposing himself to pressure; Lord Bingham favoured keeping the defence tightly confined
questions.modelAnswer: Duress is not available to a defendant who voluntarily associates with people he knows to be criminals or violent. In Hasan the House of Lords held that the test is objective as well as subjective. The defence is excluded if D foresaw, or ought reasonably to have foreseen, the risk of being subjected to any compulsion by threats of violence. He need not have foreseen being forced to commit the particular kind of offence. Lord Bingham reasoned that people who choose to associate with violent criminals bring the threat on themselves. He also saw duress as a defence open to abuse and hard for the prosecution to rebut, so it should be kept within narrow limits.

questions.q: Rhys is furious with his flatmate Tom over unpaid rent. He hits Tom hard over the head with a cast-iron frying pan, intending to kill him. Tom collapses and appears lifeless. Believing Tom is dead and panicking, Rhys drags him to a nearby river and rolls him into the water to get rid of the 'body'. In fact Tom was only unconscious, and he drowns. A week later, at a pub, Rhys argues with Tom's brother Vic and hurls a glass at him, intending to hit him. Vic ducks. The glass strikes another customer, Wendy, cutting her cheek, and then smashes a large mirror behind the bar. Rhys says he never thought about the mirror. Discuss Rhys's liability, concentrating on the general principles of coincidence of actus reus and mens rea and transferred malice. You need not consider defences.
markScheme: Identifies the coincidence problem: when Rhys had intent to kill (the blow) Tom did not die; when he did the fatal act (the river) he believed Tom was dead and had no mens rea
Applies Thabo Meli v R [1954]: a series of acts forming one transaction or plan can be treated as a whole
Notes the extension in R v Church [1966] and R v Le Brun [1992] where there was no preconceived plan, especially where the later act is an attempt to dispose of the body or conceal the crime
Causation: the blow is a factual and legal cause of death (but for; more than minimal; chain not broken by D's own act); likely conviction for murder
Wendy: intent to strike Vic transfers to Wendy under R v Latimer (1886); the cut breaks the whole skin so is a wound (JCC v Eisenhower [1984])

Identifies the appropriate offence for Wendy: battery or s47 at least; s20 if Rhys foresaw some harm (Mowatt; Savage), which throwing a glass at someone strongly suggests; s18 only if intent to do GBH
Mirror: malice does not transfer between offences of a different kind (R v Pembliton (1874)); liability for criminal damage must rest on Rhys's own recklessness under R v G [2003]
Applies R v G to his claim that he never thought about the mirror: if believed, no recklessness; the jury may disbelieve him given the setting
Clear structure: separate incidents, issue, rule, application and conclusion for each
questions.modelAnswer:
Tom's death. Rhys intended to kill when he struck Tom, but that blow did not kill. Tom died from drowning, caused by an act Rhys did while believing Tom was already dead. So at no single moment do the actus reus and mens rea of murder obviously coincide. In Thabo Meli v R [1954] the Privy Council held that a series of acts forming one plan can be treated as one transaction, so the mens rea at the start covers the whole. Rhys had no preconceived plan, but R v Church [1966] and R v Le Brun [1992] apply the same approach where the later act is part of the same sequence, particularly where D is trying to dispose of the body or cover up the attack. The blow and the dumping happened close together and the second act followed directly from the first, so a jury is entitled to treat them as one transaction. The blow was also a factual and legal cause of death, because it led directly to the drowning. Rhys is therefore likely to be guilty of murder.

Wendy. Rhys meant to hit Vic. Under R v Latimer (1886) his mens rea transfers to Wendy, because the intended and actual harm belong to the same offence. The cut breaks the whole skin, so it is a wound (JCC v Eisenhower [1984]). For s20 OAPA 1861 Rhys must have foreseen some harm (R v Mowatt [1968]; R v Savage [1992]), and anyone throwing a glass at a person almost certainly does. Section 18 would require an intention to do GBH, which is unlikely to be proved from a single throw. A s20 conviction is the probable outcome.

The mirror. Malice cannot transfer from an offence against the person to an offence against property (R v Pembliton (1874)). Rhys is guilty of criminal damage under s1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971 only if he himself was reckless under R v G [2003]: aware of a risk that property would be damaged, and unreasonable in taking it. If the jury believes that he never thought about the mirror, he is not liable. They may well reject that claim, though, given that he threw a glass in a crowded bar with a mirror behind it.

questions.q: 'Strict liability offences are an indefensible departure from the principle that criminal liability should depend on fault. Their supposed benefits are unproven, and their costs fall on the blameless.' Critically discuss this statement with reference to case law and to the arguments advanced for and against strict liability.
markScheme: Defines strict liability (no mens rea as to at least one actus reus element) and distinguishes it from absolute or situational liability (Larsonneur (1933); Winzar (1983))
Explains the presumption of mens rea: Sweet v Parsley [1970]; B v DPP [2000]; the presumption is strongest for 'truly criminal' offences
Sets out the Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v AG of Hong Kong [1985] factors: regulatory character, social concern, whether strict liability will promote the statute's purpose
Arguments for: public protection in regulated activities, encouraging high standards, efficiency of enforcement, low stigma; e.g. Alphacell v Woodward [1972] (river pollution)

Arguments against: conviction of the morally blameless, e.g. Callow v Tillstone (1900) (butcher relied on vet's certificate) and Pharmaceutical Society v Storkwain [1986]; offends the principle of individual autonomy and fair labelling
Questions the empirical claim that strict liability improves standards; those already taking all reasonable care cannot do more

Human rights dimension: R v G [2008] UKHL 37 (s5 Sexual Offences Act 2003, strict as to age) held compatible with Article 6, as Article 6 governs procedural fairness, not the substantive content of offences
Considers middle-ground solutions: due diligence or no-negligence defences, reverse burdens, confining strict liability to genuinely regulatory offences with modest penalties
Notes strict liability for serious offences (e.g. age in child sex offences) undermines the claim that it is limited to minor regulatory matters
Reaches a reasoned conclusion that engages with the quotation rather than simply describing the law
questions.modelAnswer:
Strict liability removes the need for mens rea as to at least one element of the actus reus. The courts start from a presumption that mens rea is required (Sweet v Parsley [1970]; B v DPP [2000]), and Gammon v AG of Hong Kong [1985] allows that presumption to be displaced, mainly for regulatory offences dealing with matters of social concern, and only where strict liability will actually promote the statute's purpose.

The statement is right that strict liability can convict people who are not to blame. In Callow v Tillstone (1900) a butcher who relied on a vet's certificate that meat was sound was still convicted. In Storkwain [1986] pharmacists deceived by skilful forgeries were liable. Situational cases such as Larsonneur (1933) go further and punish a state the defendant did not choose. Such convictions breach the principle that the state should not condemn people who could not have avoided the wrongdoing, and they mislabel careless or innocent people as offenders.

The statement is right too that the benefits are unproven. Strict liability is said to encourage higher standards, but someone who already takes every reasonable precaution cannot do more. The real gain is administrative: regulators do not have to prove fault in high-volume prosecutions. Supporters reply that people who choose to run risky regulated activities, like the polluting company in Alphacell v Woodward [1972], accept higher standards of responsibility, and that the low stigma of regulatory offences softens the unfairness.

The human rights challenge has largely failed. In R v G [2008] the House of Lords held that strict liability as to the child's age in s5 Sexual Offences Act 2003 is compatible with Article 6, because that Article protects fair procedure and does not dictate what offences must contain. That case also shows strict liability reaching very serious, stigmatising offences, which weakens the defence that it is confined to minor regulatory matters.

A better position is that strict liability is defensible only for genuinely regulatory offences with modest penalties, and even then a due diligence defence should normally be available, as many statutes already provide. The statement therefore overstates matters if it condemns all strict liability, but it is persuasive in its criticism of strict liability without any no-negligence defence and of its use for serious crimes.

questions.q: Gemma lives rent-free with her frail uncle Harold, on the understanding agreed between them that she will cook his meals and give him his daily heart medication. Over three weeks, absorbed in a new relationship, she stops doing either. Harold becomes weak and confused, falls and fractures his hip. A neighbour calls an ambulance. At hospital, junior doctor Jas carelessly prescribes an antibiotic to which, as Harold's notes clearly record, he is allergic; Harold suffers a serious reaction, which is treated. Five days later he dies of pneumonia. The medical evidence is that his malnourished state and immobility made pneumonia very likely, and that the allergic reaction weakened him further and 'contributed significantly' to his death. Discuss Gemma's liability for manslaughter, focusing on omissions and causation.
markScheme: States the general rule that there is no liability for omissions without a duty, and that manslaughter can be committed by omission

Duty: voluntary assumption of care for a dependant (R v Stone and Dobinson [1977]; R v Instan [1893]); the agreed arrangement for rent-free accommodation may also support a contractual-type duty (cf R v Pittwood (1902))
Breach: total failure to feed or medicate over three weeks
Factual causation: but for Gemma's omission Harold would not have become weak, fallen and contracted pneumonia when he did (R v White [1910])
Legal causation: D's conduct must be a more than minimal, operating cause; it need not be the sole cause (R v Pagett (1983))

Intervening medical negligence: R v Smith [1959] (original injury still an operating and substantial cause); R v Cheshire [1991] (chain broken only if treatment is so independent and potent as to make D's contribution insignificant); contrast R v Jordan (1956)
Applies: Jas's negligence was a significant contributor but Gemma's neglect remains an operating cause, so the chain is unlikely to be broken
Identifies the form of manslaughter: gross negligence manslaughter under R v Adomako [1995] (duty, breach, causation, gross negligence)
Risk of death must have been serious, obvious and reasonably foreseeable at the time of breach (R v Rose [2017]); likely satisfied given Harold's frailty and heart condition
Considers whether the jury would regard the negligence as so bad as to be criminal; reaches a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
English law imposes no general duty to act, but manslaughter can be committed by omission where D owes a duty. Gemma's duty arises in two ways. First, she voluntarily assumed responsibility for a dependent relative, as in R v Stone and Dobinson [1977] and R v Instan [1893], where a niece who lived with and failed to care for her aunt was liable. Secondly, the arrangement under which she lived rent-free in return for providing meals and medication resembles a contractual undertaking (compare R v Pittwood (1902)). Completely stopping both for three weeks is a clear breach.

The fall and pneumonia would not have happened as and when they did but for Gemma's neglect (R v White [1910]). Legally, her omission need only be a more than minimal cause, not the only one (R v Pagett (1983)). The difficulty is Jas's negligence. Under R v Smith [1959], D remains liable if the original harm is still an operating and substantial cause at death. R v Cheshire [1991] adds that negligent treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent of D's conduct, and so potent, that D's contribution becomes insignificant. That is rare: R v Jordan (1956), where the wound had largely healed and the treatment was palpably wrong, is the classic example. Here the medical evidence says malnourishment and immobility made pneumonia very likely. Gemma's neglect therefore remains a significant operating cause even though the allergic reaction contributed significantly. The chain is not broken.

The appropriate charge is gross negligence manslaughter under R v Adomako [1995]: duty, breach, causation and negligence so bad that the jury considers it criminal. R v Rose [2017] requires that a serious and obvious risk of death was reasonably foreseeable at the time of breach on the information then available. Gemma knew Harold was frail and needed heart medication, so withholding food and medicine for weeks plainly created an obvious risk of death. Prolonged neglect of a dependent relative for selfish reasons is exactly the kind of conduct a jury is likely to regard as gross.

Gemma is likely to be convicted of gross negligence manslaughter. Jas's carelessness may also expose Jas to separate liability, but it does not relieve Gemma.

questions.q: 'In R v G [2003] the House of Lords restored principle to the law of recklessness, but at the price of allowing the thoughtless and the indifferent to escape liability for harms that any reasonable person would have foreseen.' Critically evaluate this statement.
markScheme: Explains the subjective Cunningham [1957] test and its replacement for criminal damage by Caldwell [1982] (obvious risk not considered)
Shows the injustice of Caldwell: Elliott v C (1983), where a 14-year-old with learning difficulties was convicted for a risk she could not have appreciated
Sets out the R v G facts (two boys aged 11 and 12 set fire to newspapers, causing about £1 million of damage) and the test adopted
Explains Lord Bingham's reasons: serious crime requires a culpable state of mind; Caldwell was unfair; it misinterpreted the 1971 Act; it attracted widespread criticism
Engages with the 'thoughtless' concern: Lord Diplock's worry in Caldwell about defendants who say 'I never thought'
Notes the counterweights: juries can infer awareness and reject implausible denials; R v Parker [1977] ('closing one's mind' to an obvious risk); awareness can be fleeting
Notes intoxication: Majewski means the intoxicated defendant who fails to see a risk is still liable for basic intent offences, which closes much of the gap
Considers theoretical alternatives: Duff's concept of 'practical indifference', or a capacity-based objective test that takes account of D's characteristics
Notes that negligence-based offences (e.g. gross negligence manslaughter, careless driving) cover some inadvertent wrongdoing
Reaches a reasoned conclusion on whether the price identified in the quotation is real and acceptable
questions.modelAnswer:
Before 1982 recklessness meant conscious risk-taking (R v Cunningham [1957]). Caldwell [1982] extended it, for criminal damage, to failing to think about a risk that would have been obvious to a reasonable person. The harshness of that test was exposed in Elliott v C (1983), where a 14-year-old girl with learning difficulties, who could not have appreciated the risk, was convicted of arson. In R v G [2003] two boys aged 11 and 12 set fire to newspapers behind a shop and caused about £1 million of damage. The House of Lords restored a subjective test: D must be aware of a risk, and taking it must be unreasonable in the circumstances known to him. Lord Bingham's reasons were that conviction for serious crime should depend on a culpable state of mind, that Caldwell was unfair to young and vulnerable defendants, that it misread the 1971 Act, and that it had been widely criticised.

The first half of the statement is persuasive. R v G restores correspondence and respects the principle that people are punished for choices they made.

The second half overstates the cost. Lord Diplock's fear in Caldwell was that defendants would escape simply by claiming 'I never thought'. Juries are not bound to believe such claims and may infer awareness from the obviousness of the risk. Awareness can also be momentary, and R v Parker [1977] treats someone who closes his mind to an obvious risk as reckless. Under Majewski, voluntary intoxication is no answer to basic intent offences, so the drunk defendant who fails to notice a risk is still liable. Gross inadvertence can also be caught by negligence-based offences such as gross negligence manslaughter.

Some gap remains. A sober defendant who is truly indifferent, so that the risk never crosses his mind because he simply does not care about others' property, escapes. Duff argues that such 'practical indifference' is as culpable as conscious risk-taking. An objective test that takes account of D's capacities would catch him without repeating Elliott v C. That is a cogent point, but it is hard to prove indifference without importing the very objectivity R v G rejected.

The price identified in the quotation is real but modest, and an acceptable price for a test that ties liability to culpable choice.

questions.q: Lena is a second-year student. One evening she finds a bicycle locked outside her halls that is identical to her own. Wrongly believing it is hers and that she has lost her key, she saws through the lock. The bike and lock belong to another student, Mia. The next day, as part of a protest against tuition fees, Lena chalks large slogans on the university's stone steps; the university pays £300 for them to be jet-washed off before an open day. That afternoon she sees a dog panting heavily in a parked car on a hot day. Believing it is in danger of dying, she smashes the car window to free it. In fact the dog was not in danger, as the car's air conditioning was running. Discuss Lena's liability for criminal damage.
markScheme: States the elements of s1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971: destroying or damaging property belonging to another, without lawful excuse, intending or being reckless as to the damage and as to the property belonging to another
Lock: clearly damaged and belonging to another (s10(2)); but mens rea extends to the property belonging to another
Applies R v Smith (David) [1974]: an honest belief that the property is one's own, however mistaken, means no intention or recklessness as to damaging another's property; Lena is not guilty

Chalk: whether temporary marking is 'damage' is a matter of fact and degree; Hardman (1986) and Roe v Kingerlee [1986] show that marking which costs money to remove can be damage; contrast Morphitis v Salmon [1990]
Applies: £300 cleaning cost supports a finding of damage; Lena intended the marking; protest motive is no lawful excuse (cf AG's Reference (No 1 of 2022) on protest rights)

Window: damage to another's property intended; consider s5(2)(b): she acted to protect property (the dog is property, s10(1)) she believed was in immediate need of protection, by means she believed reasonable
s5(3): her beliefs need only be honest, not justified or reasonable; whether she acted 'in order to protect' property is objective (R v Hill and Hall (1989)) but is satisfied here
Also considers s5(2)(a): she may have believed the owner would have consented had he known the circumstances
Reasoned conclusions on each incident
questions.modelAnswer:
Under s1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971, D commits criminal damage by destroying or damaging property belonging to another, without lawful excuse, intending or being reckless both as to the damage and as to the property belonging to another.

The lock. Lena intentionally damaged the lock, and it belonged to Mia. But the mens rea covers the fact that the property belongs to someone else. In R v Smith (David) [1974] a tenant who removed panelling he honestly believed to be his own was not guilty, even though his belief rested on a mistake of law. Lena honestly believed the bike and lock were hers, so she lacked the mens rea and is not guilty. Her belief did not need to be reasonable, although a very unreasonable belief may lead a jury to doubt that she really held it.

The steps. Whether temporary marking amounts to damage is a question of fact and degree. In Hardman (1986) water-soluble paint was damage because the council had to pay to remove it, and in Roe v Kingerlee [1986] mud graffiti that cost a small sum to clean off was also damage. By contrast, harm that does not affect value or usefulness, as in Morphitis v Salmon [1990], is not damage. The university's £300 bill to make the steps presentable points strongly towards damage. Lena intended the marking, and a political motive is not a lawful excuse; AG's Reference (No 1 of 2022) shows that protest rights do not provide a defence to significant damage. She is probably guilty.

The car window. Lena intentionally damaged another's car. Under s5(2)(b) she has a lawful excuse if she acted to protect property that she believed was in immediate need of protection, by means she believed were reasonable. A dog is property (s10(1)) belonging to its owner. By s5(3) her beliefs need only be honest, so her mistake about the air conditioning does not matter. Whether she acted 'in order to protect' property is objective (R v Hill and Hall (1989)), and smashing a window to free an apparently suffering animal plainly meets that test. Alternatively, under s5(2)(a) she may have believed the owner would have consented had he known the circumstances. She is not guilty.

questions.q: Nadia, after drinking most of a bottle of wine, decides to burn her own car to claim on the insurance. She pours petrol over it as it stands in the shared parking area beneath a block of flats and sets it alight. The fire spreads to her ex-partner Owen's motorbike parked next to it, destroying it, and blackens the wall of the block, where residents are asleep. No one is hurt. Nadia says she was so drunk that she never considered the fire might spread. That weekend, in revenge, Owen throws a brick through Nadia's front window, knowing that her baby sleeps in a cot directly beneath it. Shards of glass fall into the cot, but the baby is unharmed. Discuss the liability of Nadia and Owen under the Criminal Damage Act 1971. Do not consider fraud.
markScheme: Nadia's own car: no offence under s1(1), as it is not property belonging to another; but s1(2) applies to any property, including D's own
s1(2) requires intention or recklessness as to damage and intention or recklessness as to whether life would be endangered by that damage; actual endangerment is not needed (R v Sangha [1988])
Arson: damage by fire is charged under s1(3)
Recklessness is subjective (R v G [2003]); Nadia says she did not foresee the spread

Intoxication: reckless criminal damage, including the reckless limb of s1(2), is a basic intent offence (Majewski; Caldwell [1982] on intoxication), so her drunkenness is no answer; she is treated as if she would have foreseen the risk sober
Motorbike and wall: s1(1) and s1(3) arson, reckless as to damaging property of another; again intoxication is no answer
Owen: s1(1) clearly made out for the window; s5 lawful excuse irrelevant and unavailable for s1(2)
Applies R v Steer [1988] and R v Webster; R v Warwick [1995]: danger must arise from the damage; here the danger comes from broken glass falling on the baby, so s1(2) can be made out
Owen's knowledge of the cot supports intention or at least recklessness as to endangering life by the damage
Reasoned conclusions, noting maximum of life imprisonment for s1(2) and arson
questions.modelAnswer:
Nadia. Burning her own car is not an offence under s1(1), which requires property belonging to another. Aggravated criminal damage under s1(2), however, applies to any property, including D's own. It requires (i) intention or recklessness as to destroying or damaging property and (ii) intention or recklessness as to whether life would be endangered by that destruction or damage. Because the damage was by fire, the offence is charged as arson (s1(3)). It does not matter that no one was actually endangered (R v Sangha [1988]).

Nadia intended to damage her car. The issue is whether she was reckless as to endangering life by fire spreading in a residential block at night. Recklessness is subjective (R v G [2003]), and she says she never considered the risk. However, reckless criminal damage, including the reckless limb of s1(2), is a basic intent offence: Caldwell [1982] held that self-induced intoxication is no defence to it, and that conclusion survives R v G because it rests on DPP v Majewski [1977]. Nadia is treated as if she had foreseen what she would have foreseen sober. A sober person setting fire to a car beneath occupied flats would plainly see a risk to life, so she is likely to be guilty of aggravated arson. On the same basis she is guilty of arson under s1(1) and (3) for Owen's motorbike and the wall, being reckless as to damage to property belonging to others.

Owen. Throwing a brick through the window is clearly an intentional s1(1) offence. For s1(2), R v Steer [1988] requires that the danger to life come from the damage, not from the missile. In R v Webster; R v Warwick [1995], however, the Court of Appeal held that where the damage itself, such as shattered glass or falling masonry, creates the danger, the aggravated offence is made out. Here the danger to the baby comes from the broken glass falling into the cot, which is the damage itself, not the brick. Knowing the cot was under the window, Owen at least foresaw a risk that the broken glass would endanger the baby's life, and arguably intended it. The s5 lawful excuses do not apply to s1(2) and none would fit in any event. Owen is likely to be guilty of aggravated criminal damage, which carries a maximum of life imprisonment.

questions.q: At a nightclub, Pete taps Quinn on the shoulder. When Quinn turns, Pete snarls, 'You're next. Outside in five minutes.' Quinn is frightened. Later, Pete throws the contents of his pint glass towards Quinn's group, intending to soak them with beer. The glass slips from his hand and hits Rosa, a stranger, cutting her forehead, which needs stitches. Pete says he never imagined the glass would leave his hand. When a door supervisor, Sam, takes Pete by the arm to escort him out, Pete punches Sam in the face, breaking his nose. Discuss Pete's liability for non-fatal offences against the person.
markScheme: The tap: battery requires unlawful force; Collins v Wilcock [1984] treats ordinary contact such as a tap to attract attention as impliedly consented to, so no battery
The words: assault requires V to apprehend immediate unlawful force; words can suffice (R v Ireland [1998]; R v Constanza [1997])

Immediacy: Ireland suggests fear of force within a minute or two may be immediate; 'five minutes' is borderline and should be discussed; mens rea is intention or recklessness as to Quinn's apprehension
Rosa: glass hitting her is a battery; the cut breaks the whole skin so it is a wound (JCC v Eisenhower [1984])
Mens rea for the battery: Pete intended to apply force (beer) to the group; transferred malice (R v Latimer) covers Rosa, a stranger

Applies R v Savage [1992] (almost identical facts): s47 needs only the mens rea of the battery, so s47 is made out; s20 needs foresight of some harm (Mowatt; Parmenter), which Pete denies, so a s20 conviction depends on the jury disbelieving him
Sam: punch is a battery; broken nose is at least ABH (s47); whether it is GBH depends on seriousness (DPP v Smith [1961]; R v Bollom [2003]); s20 if GBH and some harm foreseen
s18: requires intent to do GBH or to resist lawful apprehension or detention; consider whether Sam was lawfully removing a trespasser; probably s47 or s20 only
Clear structure and reasoned conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
The tap and the words. A battery is the intentional or reckless application of unlawful force. A tap on the shoulder to attract attention is the kind of ordinary contact everyone is taken to accept (Collins v Wilcock [1984]), so it is not a battery. The words may amount to an assault, which requires that Quinn apprehend immediate unlawful force. Words alone can do this (R v Constanza [1997]; R v Ireland [1998]). The difficulty is immediacy. In Ireland Lord Steyn accepted that fear of violence within a minute or two might be enough, and a threat of violence 'outside in five minutes', made face to face, is arguably close enough in time and place to qualify. Pete clearly intended to frighten Quinn, so a common assault charge under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988 is arguable.

Rosa. The glass striking Rosa is a battery, and the cut breaks the whole skin, so it is a wound (JCC v Eisenhower [1984]). Pete intended to apply force, in the form of beer, to Quinn's group. Under R v Latimer that intent transfers to Rosa, because the offence is the same. These facts closely mirror R v Savage [1992]. There the House of Lords held that s47 OAPA 1861 requires only the mens rea of the battery, so Pete is guilty of assault occasioning ABH. For s20 the prosecution must prove that Pete foresaw some physical harm (R v Mowatt [1968]; DPP v Parmenter [1992]). If the jury believes that he never thought the glass would leave his hand, he did not foresee harm, and in Savage the s20 conviction was replaced with s47 for this reason.

Sam. The punch is an intentional battery. A broken nose is at least ABH under s47. Whether it is GBH depends on whether the jury considers it really serious harm (DPP v Smith [1961]), taking account of the effect on Sam (R v Bollom [2003]). If it is GBH, s20 is made out, since anyone who punches someone in the face foresees some harm. Section 18 would require an intention to do GBH or to resist lawful detention. Removing Pete from the club is not a lawful arrest, and a single punch is weak evidence of intent to do serious harm. The likely outcome is s47, or s20 if the injury is judged serious.

questions.q: 'The law on consent to bodily harm, as laid down in R v Brown [1994], is incoherent in its exceptions and paternalistic in its foundations.' Critically discuss.
markScheme: States the general rule: consent is a defence to assault and battery but not to ABH or worse unless within a recognised exception (AG's Reference (No 6 of 1980); Brown)

Explains the majority's reasoning in Brown (public interest, risk of escalation and infection, corruption of the young) and the dissents of Lords Mustill and Slynn (private conduct, not the business of the criminal law)
Identifies the exceptions: properly conducted sport (R v Barnes [2004]), surgery, tattooing and piercing, horseplay (R v Jones (1986); R v Aitken [1992]), and personal adornment (R v Wilson [1996])

Incoherence: Wilson (branding) versus Brown and R v Emmett [1999]; reckless injury in drunken horseplay allowed while consensual sexual activity is not; R v BM [2018] (body modification outside the tattooing exception)
Contrast with consent to risk of infection in Dica [2004] and Konzani [2005], which permits informed consent to risk of serious harm
Paternalism and moralism: Mill's harm principle and autonomy versus legal moralism (Devlin) and public interest; Laskey, Jaggard and Brown v UK (1997) found no breach of Article 8
Recent statutory endorsement: s71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 codifies the Brown position for sexual gratification, in response to the 'rough sex defence', with an STI exception
Considers the protective rationale: difficulty of proving genuine consent, especially in domestic abuse contexts
Considers reform options (e.g. Law Commission Consultation Paper No 139 (1995) proposed allowing consent to injuries short of seriously disabling injury)
Reasoned conclusion engaging with both limbs of the quotation
questions.modelAnswer:
Consent is a defence to common assault and battery, but under AG's Reference (No 6 of 1980) and R v Brown [1994] it does not excuse ABH or more serious harm unless the activity falls within a recognised public-interest exception. The Brown majority refused to create an exception for sadomasochism, citing the risks of escalation and infection and the corruption of young men. Lords Mustill and Slynn dissented, treating the conduct as private and outside the proper concern of the criminal law.

The charge of incoherent exceptions is well founded. Rough horseplay that causes serious injury can be consented to (R v Jones (1986); R v Aitken [1992]), and so can the risks of contact sport (R v Barnes [2004]). Yet consensual sexual activity causing lesser harm cannot. Wilson [1996] allowed a husband to brand his wife as 'personal adornment', but Emmett [1999] refused consent for burns and asphyxiation within a relationship. R v BM [2018] held that body modification such as ear removal does not fall within the tattooing exception, which suggests that the boundaries depend on judicial comfort with the activity rather than on the degree of harm. Dica [2004] and Konzani [2005] allow informed consent to a risk of serious disease during sex, which sits awkwardly with refusing consent to deliberate, more minor injuries.

The charge of paternalism is more contestable. On a Millian view, harm to consenting adults is not the state's business, and Lord Templeman's language in Brown reflects legal moralism of the kind Devlin defended. The Strasbourg court in Laskey v UK (1997) nonetheless found the convictions a proportionate interference with Article 8. There is also a protective rationale: whether consent was genuine is hard to prove, especially in abusive relationships. Parliament endorsed that concern in s71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021, which codified Brown for sexual gratification after concern about the so-called 'rough sex defence'.

A more principled scheme would allow consent to all but seriously disabling injury, as the Law Commission suggested in Consultation Paper No 139 (1995), while keeping safeguards about the quality of consent. The quotation is persuasive as to incoherence. As to paternalism it is only partly right, because the modern justification rests more on protecting people from abuse than on morals.

questions.q: Uma wants to frighten her neighbour Viktor, whom she blames for her dog's death. Late at night she pours petrol through his letterbox and sets it alight, intending only to 'give him a scare'. She knows Viktor and his teenage son live there and are likely to be asleep. The fire spreads quickly; Viktor escapes but his son dies of smoke inhalation. At trial, Uma says she expected the smoke alarm to wake them and that she 'didn't want anyone hurt'. Discuss whether Uma has the mens rea for murder, and what the jury should be told.
markScheme: States the actus reus of murder (unlawful killing of a human being under the King's peace) and causation (fire a factual and legal cause of death)
Mens rea: malice aforethought means intention to kill or to cause GBH (R v Vickers [1957]; R v Cunningham [1982])
No direct intention: Uma's purpose was to frighten

Oblique intention: Woollin [1999] direction based on Nedrick [1986]: jury not entitled to find intention unless death or serious injury was a virtual certainty (barring some unforeseen intervention) and Uma appreciated that
Notes the similar facts of Nedrick and Hyam v DPP [1975], and that Hyam's 'high probability' approach no longer represents the law
Applies: setting fire to an occupied house at night strongly suggests serious injury was virtually certain; but her belief about the smoke alarm goes to whether she appreciated it
Matthews and Alleyne [2003]: even if the conditions are met, the jury may, but need not, find intention
Alternative: if intention is not found, unlawful act manslaughter (arson is a dangerous unlawful act under Church [1966])
Reasoned conclusion on likely verdict and the direction to give
questions.modelAnswer:
Uma caused the son's death, because the fire was both the factual and the legal cause of it. The issue is malice aforethought, which means an intention to kill or to cause GBH (R v Vickers [1957]; R v Cunningham [1982]). Uma's purpose was to frighten Viktor, so she had no direct intention, and the question is oblique intention.

The jury should be given the Woollin [1999] direction, which builds on Nedrick [1986], a case with very similar letterbox-arson facts. They are not entitled to find that Uma intended death or serious injury unless (i) death or serious bodily harm was a virtual certainty, barring some unforeseen intervention, as a result of her actions, and (ii) she appreciated that this was the case. In Hyam v DPP [1975], another letterbox fire case, foresight of high probability was treated as enough, but after Moloney [1985] and Woollin that is no longer the law.

On the first limb, setting fire to petrol in the hallway of an occupied house at night when the occupants are likely to be asleep makes serious injury close to inevitable, so the jury may well find virtual certainty. The second limb is more open. Uma says she expected the smoke alarm to wake them and did not want anyone hurt. If the jury thinks she may genuinely have believed the occupants would escape unharmed, she did not appreciate a virtual certainty of serious harm. If they think that belief is implausible, they may conclude she must have appreciated it. Even if both limbs are satisfied, R v Matthews and Alleyne [2003] confirms that the jury may find intention but is not obliged to.

If the jury does not find intention, Uma is clearly guilty of unlawful act manslaughter. Arson is a crime, it is objectively dangerous under R v Church [1966], and it caused death. The jury should be told about both verdicts. Murder is a realistic possibility, but manslaughter is a likely compromise if they accept her account of the smoke alarm.

questions.q: Wes, 19, and Xander, 17, break into a terraced house at 2am to steal electronics, believing it to be empty. In the hallway they come face to face with the occupier, Yvonne, aged 82, who is visibly frail and walking with a frame. Wes shouts abuse at her and throws a vase that smashes on the wall beside her. They flee. Yvonne, terrified, suffers a heart attack and dies an hour later. Separately, Xander's older sister Zara, a nurse, had earlier sold Xander some prescription painkillers she had taken from work. Xander gave two tablets to his friend Abe, who swallowed them with alcohol and died. Discuss the liability of Wes and Xander for Yvonne's death and of Zara and Xander for Abe's death.
markScheme: Identifies unlawful act manslaughter as the relevant offence for Yvonne (no intent to kill or cause GBH, so not murder)
Unlawful act: burglary, criminal damage (the vase) and assault; each is a crime with its own mens rea (R v Lamb [1967])
Dangerousness: R v Church [1966] objective test; sober and reasonable bystander with D's knowledge, including knowledge gained during the act
Contrasts R v Dawson (1985) (no knowledge of the victim's frailty) with R v Watson [1989] (frailty apparent during burglary, so the act became dangerous); Yvonne's frailty was obvious
Shock causing death can be 'physical harm' (Watson; Dawson); thin skull rule (R v Blaue [1975]) and causation

Xander's liability as a joint participant: R v Jogee [2016] (secondary liability requires intentional assistance or encouragement with intent; foresight is evidence only) or as a co-principal in the burglary; consider whether the assault by Wes was within the common purpose

Abe: unlawful act manslaughter requires an unlawful act that causes death; supplying a controlled drug may be unlawful, but R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] holds that Abe's free, deliberate and informed self-administration breaks the chain
Zara: further removed again; supply to Xander and then from Xander to Abe; no causation
Gross negligence manslaughter by omission (R v Evans [2009]) is not on the facts, as neither Xander nor Zara was present or aware of a life-threatening state; R v Adomako [1995] would require a duty
Notes any other liability (e.g. supply offences under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 or theft) without extended discussion; reasoned conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
Yvonne's death. Neither burglar intended to kill or cause GBH, so the relevant offence is unlawful act manslaughter. That requires a deliberate criminal act (R v Lamb [1967]), which must be objectively dangerous (R v Church [1966]) and must cause death. The burglary, Wes's assault and the criminal damage to the vase are all crimes.

Dangerousness is judged by a sober and reasonable bystander with the knowledge D had or would have gained during the act. In R v Dawson (1985) the conviction was quashed because nothing showed that the petrol station attendant had a heart condition. In R v Watson [1989], by contrast, the burglars must have seen that the occupier was frail and elderly, so the burglary became dangerous once they saw him. Yvonne was visibly frail and using a walking frame. A reasonable person seeing that would recognise that shouting abuse at her and throwing a vase near her carried a risk of physical harm from shock. Watson also accepts that a heart attack caused by fright can amount to physical harm. Causation is satisfied: the thin skull rule (R v Blaue [1975]) means Yvonne's frailty does not help Wes, though Watson's own conviction was quashed on causation, so the medical evidence will matter. Wes is likely to be guilty of manslaughter.

Xander's position depends on whether he was a joint principal in a dangerous unlawful act or a secondary party to Wes's assault. Under R v Jogee [2016] secondary liability requires intentional assistance or encouragement with the relevant intent. Foresight that Wes might act violently is only evidence of that intent. If Xander shared in the burglary while the confrontation developed, and continued after seeing Yvonne's frailty, he may also be a party to a dangerous unlawful act. If Wes's outburst was a spontaneous act Xander did not encourage, Xander's liability is doubtful.

Abe's death. Supplying a controlled drug can be an unlawful act. But R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] holds that the free, deliberate and informed act of a fully informed adult who takes the drug himself breaks the chain of causation. Abe chose to swallow the tablets, so Xander did not cause his death in law. Zara is even further removed. Gross negligence manslaughter by omission under R v Evans [2009] would require awareness of a life-threatening state, and neither of them was present. Neither is liable for manslaughter.

questions.q: 'The law of murder in England and Wales is too broad at its base and too rigid at its top. The 'GBH rule' sweeps in killers who never contemplated death, while the mandatory life sentence prevents any distinction between them and the most culpable.' Critically discuss with reference to case law and reform proposals.
markScheme: Explains malice aforethought: intention to kill or cause GBH; Vickers [1957], Cunningham [1982], confirmed in Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 1994) [1998] and R v Powell and English [1999] discussion
Critique of the GBH rule: departs from correspondence; constructive liability for the gravest offence; Lord Steyn's criticism in Powell and English; Lord Mustill in AG's Ref (No 3 of 1994)
Defence of the GBH rule: one who intends really serious harm accepts a risk of death; fair labelling arguments; its role in capturing culpable killers
Breadth also through oblique intention: Woollin's 'evidence' approach and jury discretion; risk of inconsistency
Rigidity: mandatory life sentence under the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965; minimum terms now set by Schedule 21 Sentencing Act 2020, providing some differentiation
Partial defences (loss of control, diminished responsibility, suicide pact) exist largely because of the mandatory sentence

Reform: Law Commission, Murder, Manslaughter and Infanticide (Law Com No 304, 2006): three-tier structure with first degree murder (intent to kill, or intent to cause serious injury with awareness of serious risk of death) and second degree murder (including intent to cause serious injury), mandatory life only for first degree
Government's non-implementation of the three-tier scheme, though partial defences were reformed by the Coroners and Justice Act 2009
Evaluates competing views (e.g. Ashworth on correspondence; Horder on fair labelling); considers whether broadening manslaughter is a better solution
Reasoned conclusion engaging with both halves of the quotation
questions.modelAnswer:
Malice aforethought includes an intention to cause GBH (R v Vickers [1957]; R v Cunningham [1982]). A defendant who intends a serious but non-lethal injury, and never thinks about death, is therefore a murderer if V dies. That breaks the principle of correspondence and makes the most serious offence partly constructive. Lord Mustill in AG's Reference (No 3 of 1994) [1998] criticised the rule as anomalous, and Lord Steyn in R v Powell and English [1999] urged Parliament to reconsider it.

The rule has defenders. Someone who sets out to cause really serious harm deliberately attacks another's bodily integrity and accepts a real chance that the victim will die. Fair labelling may support calling such a killer a murderer. The rule is also practical, because juries find it easier to decide intended serious harm than foresight of death. But the definition of GBH, 'really serious harm', includes injuries such as a broken limb that carry little risk of death, so the rule can catch people of quite different culpability.

The top of the offence is rigid because of the mandatory life sentence. Schedule 21 Sentencing Act 2020 allows judges to vary the minimum term, and an intention to cause only serious harm is a mitigating factor. That reduces the sentencing problem, but the label and the life licence still apply to everyone convicted of murder. The partial defences of loss of control and diminished responsibility exist mainly to avoid the mandatory sentence, which shows how much distortion it causes.

The Law Commission's Murder, Manslaughter and Infanticide (Law Com No 304, 2006) proposed three tiers. First degree murder, carrying the mandatory sentence, would require an intention to kill, or an intention to cause serious injury with awareness of a serious risk of death. Second degree murder would cover an intention to cause serious injury, among other states of mind, with a discretionary life maximum. Below these would sit manslaughter. The scheme would reserve the mandatory sentence for the most culpable while keeping the murder label for serious harm killers. Parliament reformed only the partial defences, through the Coroners and Justice Act 2009.

The statement is largely persuasive. The real problem is the combination of a wide offence and a fixed sentence. Either narrowing the GBH rule or removing the mandatory sentence would ease it, and the Law Commission's graded structure deals with both.

questions.q: Bea works in a bookshop. She takes a £20 note from the till, intending to buy lunch and replace it from her wages on Friday, as she has done before without the manager noticing. Later, a customer, Cal, leaves an expensive umbrella behind; Bea takes it home, reasoning that 'nobody ever comes back for these'. The shop has a lost property box and Cal's name is written inside the umbrella. Finally, Bea borrows a hardback from the shop's stock to read over the weekend, intending to return it on Monday. Discuss whether Bea has committed theft.
markScheme: States s1 Theft Act 1968 and its five elements
£20: appropriation (s3; Morris), property (s4, money), belonging to another (the shop)
Intention to permanently deprive: she intends to replace equivalent money, not the same note; R v Velumyl [1989] holds this is still an intention to permanently deprive of the specific property
s2(2): willingness to pay does not prevent dishonesty; s2(1)(b) belief in consent unlikely given concealment; apply Ivey/Barton and Booth
Umbrella: property belonging to Cal (s5(1)); appropriation by taking it home
s2(1)(c): not dishonest if she believed the owner could not be discovered by taking reasonable steps; name inside and lost property box make the belief unlikely to be genuine

Book: appropriation and property belonging to another, but intention to permanently deprive is doubtful; s6 and R v Lloyd [1985]: borrowing counts only if the goodness or virtue is exhausted; reading a book does not exhaust its value
Even if dishonest, no theft of the book; reasoned conclusions on all three items
questions.modelAnswer:
Theft requires dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it (s1 Theft Act 1968).

The £20. Taking the note is an appropriation, because it assumes the owner's rights (s3; R v Morris [1984]), and the money is property belonging to the shop. Bea intends to repay an equivalent sum, not to return the same note. In R v Velumyl [1989] a manager who took money from the safe intending to replace it later had the intention to permanently deprive the company of the actual notes taken. Under s2(2), being willing to pay does not stop the appropriation being dishonest. Bea cannot realistically claim to believe the shop would consent (s2(1)(b)) when she keeps it from the manager. Under Ivey v Genting [2017], as applied in Barton and Booth [2020], ordinary decent people would probably regard secretly helping herself to the till as dishonest. She is likely guilty.

The umbrella. It is property belonging to Cal (s5(1)), and taking it home is an appropriation. Under s2(1)(c) she is not dishonest if she believed the owner could not be discovered by taking reasonable steps. The question is whether she genuinely held that belief, not whether it was reasonable, but its unreasonableness is evidence that she did not. Cal's name is inside the umbrella and the shop has a lost property box, so a jury is unlikely to accept that she held the belief. If s2 does not apply, the Ivey test probably finds her dishonest. She is likely guilty.

The book. Taking the book is an appropriation of property belonging to the shop, but Bea intends to return it. Section 6 treats borrowing as an intention to permanently deprive only where it amounts to an outright taking. R v Lloyd [1985] held that this means returning the thing with all its goodness or virtue gone. Reading a hardback over a weekend leaves it essentially unchanged, although it might no longer be saleable as new if it is visibly worn. There is probably no intention to permanently deprive, so there is no theft of the book. Bea may still face disciplinary consequences.

questions.q: Dev believes his former landlord, Ed, wrongly kept his £800 deposit. One evening Dev goes to Ed's house to 'get my money back'. Ed's door is open; Dev walks in uninvited, intending to take £800 in cash if he finds it. In the hallway he finds Ed's wallet containing £300, which he pockets. Ed appears and grabs Dev's arm; Dev shoves Ed hard against the wall and runs off with the wallet. Ed is bruised. It later emerges that Dev's deposit had been lawfully retained to cover damage, and Dev had been told this in writing. Discuss Dev's liability for burglary, theft and robbery.
markScheme: Theft elements; s2(1)(a): not dishonest if D believed he had a legal right to deprive the other; the belief need only be genuine (R v Robinson [1977])
Notes the belief must be in a legal right, not a moral one; the written notice is evidence the belief was not genuine, but genuineness is a question of fact (Ivey: actual state of mind)
Notes the wallet itself (not just cash): Dev took the wallet and the extra items, which goes beyond any claimed right to £800 cash; dishonesty as to the wallet
If no dishonesty, no theft, therefore no robbery (Robinson) and no burglary under s9(1)(b) based on theft

Robbery: s8; force must be used immediately before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal; R v Hale (1978): appropriation is continuing; shove while making off with the wallet is likely 'at the time of' stealing
Force on a person: shove clearly sufficient (R v Dawson and James (1976); R v Clouden [1987])

Burglary s9(1)(a): entry as a trespasser into a building with intent to steal; Dev entered uninvited, knowing or reckless as to trespass (R v Collins [1973]); conditional intent to steal if he finds cash is sufficient (AG's References (Nos 1 and 2 of 1979))
Burglary s9(1)(b): having entered as a trespasser, steals; and consider whether shove amounts to inflicting GBH (no: bruising is not GBH)
Dishonesty under Ivey/Barton and Booth applies to all; reasoned conclusions depending on the jury's finding on Dev's belief
questions.modelAnswer:
Theft. Dev appropriated the wallet and cash, which were property belonging to Ed, intending to keep them. The key issue is dishonesty. Under s2(1)(a) Theft Act 1968 he is not dishonest if he believed he had a legal right to deprive Ed of the property, and the belief need only be genuine (R v Robinson [1977]). The written explanation that the deposit was lawfully kept is strong evidence that he did not genuinely believe in a legal right. However, under Ivey v Genting [2017] the question is his actual state of mind. Even if he did believe he was owed £800, that would hardly explain taking the wallet itself. The jury may well find him dishonest at least as to the wallet. If they do not, the s2 belief would defeat both theft and robbery, as it did in Robinson.

Robbery. Under s8, D commits robbery if he steals and, immediately before or at the time of doing so, uses force on a person in order to steal. In R v Hale (1978) appropriation was treated as a continuing act, so force used while D is still making off with the property can be 'at the time of' the theft. Dev shoved Ed while escaping with the wallet in order to keep it. A hard shove is clearly enough force (R v Dawson and James (1976); R v Clouden [1987]). If theft is proved, Dev is likely guilty of robbery.

Burglary. Under s9(1)(a), D commits burglary if he enters a building as a trespasser intending to steal. Dev entered without permission and knew he was not invited, which satisfies R v Collins [1973]. His intention to take cash if he found any is a conditional intention, which is sufficient (AG's References (Nos 1 and 2 of 1979)), subject to the same dishonesty point. Under s9(1)(b), having entered as a trespasser, he then stole. Bruising is not GBH, so the GBH limb does not apply. Because the house is a dwelling, the higher maximum of 14 years applies.

If the jury rejects his claimed belief, Dev is likely guilty of burglary and robbery. If they accept that he may genuinely have believed he had a legal right to the cash, the charges become harder to prove, though the wallet itself still poses a problem for him.

questions.q: 'After DPP v Gomez [1993] and R v Hinks [2001], appropriation is a neutral concept that does almost no work, leaving the jury's judgment of dishonesty to decide whether a crime has been committed. Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] has made this problem worse, not better.' Critically discuss.
markScheme: Explains s3(1) and the meaning of appropriation: Morris [1984] (any assumption of any right), and the conflict over consent
Lawrence v MPC [1972] and Gomez [1993]: appropriation does not require absence of consent; consent obtained by deception is irrelevant
Hinks [2001]: receiving a valid, indefeasible gift can be appropriation; dissent of Lord Hobhouse; criticism (e.g. Sir John Smith) of conflict with civil law
Consequence: almost any dealing with another's property is an appropriation; dishonesty becomes the main filter
Overlap with fraud and obtaining by deception; theft and fraud largely cover the same ground
Pre-Ivey: Ghosh [1982] two-stage test with subjective second limb; criticisms (Robin Hood defence, uneven standards)
Ivey (obiter) and Barton and Booth [2020]: second limb removed; purely objective standard of ordinary decent people once D's beliefs are found

Arguments that Ivey worsens the problem: an objective standard gives the jury still less guidance and less connection to D's own appreciation, increasing the risk of convicting people who did not see themselves as dishonest; uncertainty and inconsistency between juries

Arguments that Ivey improves matters: removes a defendant-centred standard that allowed idiosyncratic moral views to excuse; aligns with civil law (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995]); s2 still protects key beliefs
ECHR/legal certainty: concerns about Article 7 and dishonesty as an open-textured standard
Reasoned conclusion on both claims
questions.modelAnswer:
Section 3(1) Theft Act 1968 defines appropriation as any assumption of the rights of an owner, and Morris [1984] held that assuming any one right is enough. Lawrence v MPC [1972] and DPP v Gomez [1993] went further and held that an act authorised by the owner, even with consent obtained by deception, is still an appropriation. Hinks [2001] then held that accepting a gift that is valid in civil law, and which passes an unchallengeable title, can be an appropriation too. Lord Hobhouse dissented, arguing that it is wrong to treat as theft the receipt of property the civil law says the defendant now owns.

The first claim is therefore largely right. After Gomez, a shopper who simply takes goods from a shelf appropriates them, so appropriation filters out almost nothing. The real line between a shopper and a thief, or between a lucky beneficiary and a predatory carer, is drawn by dishonesty.

Whether Ivey has made things worse is more debatable. Under R v Ghosh [1982] the jury asked whether the conduct was dishonest by ordinary standards and whether D realised that ordinary people would see it that way. Ivey, obiter, and R v Barton and Booth [2020] removed the second question. The jury now finds D's actual beliefs about the facts and then applies the standards of ordinary decent people. Critics say this widens liability: a defendant who honestly but unusually thought his conduct acceptable can now be convicted, and in an area where appropriation already does so little, more depends on an undefined community standard that varies between juries. It also strains Article 7's requirement of legal certainty.

There are good responses. The Ghosh second limb allowed a defendant's warped moral views to excuse him and puzzled juries. The Ivey test brings the criminal law into line with the civil law (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995]), and D's real beliefs about the facts still count. Section 2 continues to protect the most important honest beliefs, such as a claim of right.

The first claim is convincing, and Ivey has sharpened the dependence on dishonesty without causing it. The root problem is the breadth given to appropriation by Gomez and Hinks, and a narrower concept of appropriation would ease the pressure on dishonesty.

questions.q: Faye runs an online business selling 'designer' handbags that she knows are counterfeit, describing them on her website as 'authentic, with certificate'. Gil, a buyer, knows they are fake and buys one anyway as a joke gift. Faye also pays for her groceries with a debit card she found in the street, using contactless payment. Separately, Faye's elderly neighbour Hana has given her a power of attorney to manage her finances. Faye transfers £5,000 from Hana's account to her own, intending to repay it next month from expected business profits. Faye also failed to tell her landlord, as required by a clause in her lease, that she had started running a business from the flat. Discuss Faye's liability under the Fraud Act 2006.
markScheme: s2: website description is an express false representation that Faye knows is untrue; intent to make a gain (the price)
No one need be deceived: fraud is complete on making the representation; Gil's knowledge is irrelevant to liability under s2
Dishonesty under Ivey/Barton and Booth: selling known fakes as authentic plainly dishonest
Debit card: using it impliedly represents authority to use it (MPC v Charles [1977]; R v Lambie [1982]); representation to a machine or system (s2(5)); gain of goods/money
Also possible theft of the card and of the money; notes that ss6-7 and s11 may be relevant (e.g. s6 possession of an article for use in fraud)
Hana: s4 abuse of position; a power of attorney is a classic position in which D is expected to safeguard another's financial interests
Abuse: transfer for her own benefit; intention to make a gain (s5 includes temporary gain) and cause loss
Dishonesty: intention to repay does not prevent dishonesty; apply Ivey; jury likely to find dishonest given the lack of authority and risk to Hana
Lease clause: s3 requires a legal duty to disclose (contractual duty suffices) and intention to gain or cause loss through non-disclosure; consider whether the intent is satisfied
Reasoned conclusions for each
questions.modelAnswer:
The handbags. Describing the bags as 'authentic, with certificate' is an express representation of fact that Faye knows is untrue. She makes it intending to gain the purchase price, which is money within s5. Fraud under s2 is a conduct crime, so it is complete once she dishonestly makes the representation with that intention. It does not matter that Gil was not deceived. Applying Ivey v Genting [2017] and Barton and Booth [2020], ordinary decent people would regard selling known counterfeits as authentic as dishonest. Every listing on the website is a separate potential offence.

The debit card. Using a card impliedly represents that the user has authority to use it (MPC v Charles [1977]; R v Lambie [1982]). Faye has no such authority, so the representation is false. Under s2(5) a representation can be made to a machine or system, which covers contactless payment. She intends to gain the groceries and to cause loss to the cardholder or bank. She is guilty under s2, and keeping the card may also be theft and possession of an article for use in fraud under s6.

Hana's money. Section 4 applies where D occupies a position in which she is expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests and dishonestly abuses it. A power of attorney is a clear example. Transferring £5,000 to herself is an abuse, and s5 includes temporary gain and loss, so it does not help Faye that she meant to repay. Her intention to repay goes to dishonesty, but her lack of authority and the risk to Hana, given that repayment depends on uncertain profits, mean a jury is likely to find her dishonest. Theft of the credit balance is an alternative charge.

The lease. Section 3 requires dishonest failure to disclose information that D is under a legal duty to disclose. A contractual term creates such a duty. The prosecution must also prove that Faye intended, by not disclosing, to make a gain or cause loss, for example by avoiding a rent increase or the termination of her lease. If that intent is shown and she is found dishonest, s3 is made out. Otherwise this is a civil breach only.

questions.q: 'By abolishing the need for deception, obtaining or loss, the Fraud Act 2006 has turned fraud into an inchoate offence in all but name, and has come dangerously close to criminalising mere lying.' Critically evaluate this assessment of the Fraud Act 2006.
markScheme: Background: the deception offences under the Theft Acts 1968 and 1978; technical problems such as the difficulty of 'deceiving' a machine and R v Preddy [1996] (no property 'belonging to another' obtained in bank transfers); Law Commission Report No 276 (2002)
Structure of the 2006 Act: single fraud offence with three modes (ss2-4), plus ss6, 7 and 11
Conduct-crime nature: liability attaches at the point of representation; no need for anyone to be deceived or for property to be obtained
Comparison with inchoate offences: it criminalises conduct before harm, like attempt, but without the 'more than merely preparatory' threshold; Ormerod's critique of over-criminalisation
Limiting factors: representation must be false and D must know it is or might be; dishonesty; intention to gain or cause loss in money or property (s5)
Dishonesty as the key filter: after Ivey and Barton and Booth, an objective standard; risks of uncertainty and over-reliance on juries
s3 limited to legal duty; s4 'abuse of position' arguably vague (R v Valujevs [2014] not confined to fiduciary relationships)
Benefits: removes technicality (Preddy problems), covers machine fraud (s2(5)), adapts to online and phishing fraud; prosecutorial efficiency
Counterarguments: lying is criminal only with dishonest intent to gain or cause loss in property terms; many lies (e.g. social, puffery) remain outside
Reasoned conclusion assessing the claim
questions.modelAnswer:
Before 2006, fraud was prosecuted mainly through the deception offences in the Theft Acts 1968 and 1978. These required a person to be deceived and property or another benefit to be obtained, which caused technical problems. It was doubtful whether a machine could be deceived. In R v Preddy [1996] the House of Lords held that obtaining a mortgage advance by bank transfer was not obtaining property belonging to another. Following Law Com No 276 (2002), the Fraud Act 2006 created one offence that can be committed by false representation (s2), failure to disclose (s3) or abuse of position (s4).

The 'inchoate in all but name' claim has force. Section 2 is complete as soon as the false representation is made. Nothing need be believed, obtained or lost. In practice the offence punishes an attempt to gain by deceit, without the 'more than merely preparatory' threshold that limits criminal attempts. Ormerod and others argue this pushes liability very far back and weakens the link between crime and harm. Sections 6 and 7 (articles for use in fraud) go further still.

The 'mere lying' claim is overstated. Several limits remain. The representation must be false and D must know it is or might be. D must intend to make a gain or cause loss, and s5 restricts gain and loss to money or other property. D must also be dishonest. Social lies, sales puffery and lies told with no aim of financial gain or loss fall outside the offence. The real concern is that dishonesty does most of the filtering. After Ivey and Barton and Booth that judgment is objective and undefined, so whether a lie becomes fraud depends heavily on the jury. Section 4 adds vagueness: Valujevs [2014] did not confine 'position' to fiduciary relationships.

The Act does solve real problems. It removes the Preddy difficulties, expressly covers representations to machines (s2(5)), and fits online and phishing fraud well.

The assessment is right that fraud now works much like an inchoate offence, and that the dishonesty standard is doing a great deal of work. It is wrong to say the Act criminalises mere lying, because the requirement of an intended financial gain or loss in property terms still limits the offence. The better criticism concerns how wide and uncertain the dishonesty filter is, not the decision to abandon a deception requirement.

questions.q: Ian, who has type 1 diabetes, injects his insulin before a party but then eats almost nothing and drinks six pints of lager. He knows from previous episodes and medical advice that skipping food after insulin can make him confused and aggressive. Later, in a confused state, he punches Jack, breaking his jaw. Medical evidence is unclear whether his confusion was due mainly to hypoglycaemia or to alcohol. The following week, Ian's friend Kim, as a joke, secretly adds vodka to Ian's soft drink. Ian, knowing he is getting drunk but not why, gets into an argument and smashes Kim's phone deliberately. Discuss Ian's liability and any defences.
markScheme: Jack: s20 or s18 (broken jaw likely GBH); identify the mens rea issues

Automatism: total loss of voluntary control required (Bratty [1963]; AG's Ref (No 2 of 1992)); hypoglycaemia caused by insulin is an external factor, so sane automatism (R v Quick [1973]) rather than insanity (contrast R v Hennessy [1989])

Self-induced automatism: R v Bailey [1983]; defence to specific intent offences (s18); for basic intent offences (s20) unavailable if D was reckless, i.e. knew his conduct could make him aggressive, unpredictable or uncontrolled; R v Hardie [1985]
Applies: Ian knew from experience that skipping food made him aggressive, so is reckless; no defence to s20

Intoxication: voluntary intoxication relevant only to specific intent (Majewski); combined causes: courts approach mixed intoxication and other conditions carefully (cf R v Coley, McGhee and Harris [2013]; Dietschmann for diminished responsibility)
Likely outcome: no defence to s20; possible acquittal of s18 if he lacked intent to do GBH
Phone: criminal damage under s1(1) CDA 1971; involuntary intoxication from a spiked drink
R v Kingston [1995]: if Ian formed the intent (he smashed the phone deliberately), involuntary intoxication is no defence; a drunken intent is still an intent
R v Allen [1988] distinction: knowing he was drinking alcohol but not its strength is voluntary; here he did not know alcohol was present at all, so it is involuntary, but irrelevant given intent
Reasoned conclusion; evaluation of the policy of Majewski/Bailey
questions.modelAnswer:
Jack. A broken jaw is likely to be GBH, so s20 and s18 OAPA 1861 are both relevant. Ian may argue automatism, which requires a total loss of voluntary control (Bratty [1963]; AG's Reference (No 2 of 1992)). Confusion alone will not be enough. If his condition was hypoglycaemia caused by insulin, that is an external cause, so the case is one of sane automatism (R v Quick [1973]), not insanity as in R v Hennessy [1989], where hyperglycaemia came from the disease itself.

The automatism was self-induced. Under R v Bailey [1983], self-induced automatism not caused by drink or drugs is a defence to a specific intent offence such as s18. It is also a defence to a basic intent offence such as s20 unless D was reckless, meaning he knew that his acts or omissions might make him aggressive, unpredictable or uncontrolled (see also R v Hardie [1985]). Ian knew from previous episodes and medical advice that not eating after insulin made him aggressive, so he was reckless. Automatism is no defence to s20.

The alcohol complicates matters. Under DPP v Majewski [1977] voluntary intoxication is relevant only to whether he formed a specific intent. In R v Coley, McGhee and Harris [2013] the Court of Appeal indicated that where the condition is induced by voluntary intoxication, the intoxication rules govern, not automatism. Whichever cause predominated, then, Ian has no defence to s20. On s18, the jury must be sure he actually intended GBH, and his confused state may leave doubt. The likely result is conviction under s20 and acquittal of s18.

The phone. Smashing Kim's phone deliberately is criminal damage under s1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971. Ian did not know there was alcohol in his drink, so his intoxication was involuntary. This is unlike R v Allen [1988], where D knew he was drinking alcohol but misjudged its strength. However, R v Kingston [1995] holds that involuntary intoxication is a defence only if D lacked the mens rea, because a drunken intent is still an intent. Ian acted deliberately, so he intended the damage and is guilty. His involuntary intoxication can only mitigate sentence.

These rules reflect policy rather than strict subjectivism. They allocate responsibility to people who carelessly bring about their own incapacity, but they make liability depend on fine and sometimes arbitrary distinctions.

questions.q: 'The rules on voluntary intoxication in English criminal law, built on DPP v Majewski [1977], are an unprincipled compromise: they abandon the subjective approach to mens rea for policy reasons without any coherent test for when they apply.' Critically discuss, with reference to case law and reform proposals.
markScheme: States the Majewski rule and the specific/basic intent distinction, with examples
Identifies the competing justifications: Lord Elwyn-Jones's view that becoming intoxicated is a reckless course of conduct supplying the mens rea; public protection; prior fault
Criticism: the prior fault is not temporally or substantively linked to the later offence; violates coincidence and correspondence; one who drinks is not thereby reckless as to a specific harm

Lack of a coherent test: specific intent variously described as offences requiring purposive intent or ulterior intent (R v Heard [2007]); Heard held sexual touching is basic intent while recognising that some intentional offences are treated as basic intent

Inconsistent applications: Jaggard v Dickinson [1981] (intoxicated belief supports s5 CDA defence) versus R v O'Grady [1987], R v Hatton [2005] and s76(5) CJIA 2008 (intoxicated mistake cannot ground self-defence even for murder)
Involuntary intoxication: Kingston [1995] (drunken intent is intent); Hardie [1985] and Allen [1988] distinctions; Gallagher [1963] (Dutch courage)

Alternative views: full subjectivity, admitting intoxication evidence for all offences (the Australian High Court in R v O'Connor (1980)), or a separate offence of dangerous intoxication (proposed by the Butler Committee, 1975)

Law Commission, Intoxication and Criminal Liability (Law Com No 314, 2009): proposed replacing specific/basic labels with a test based on whether the fault element is an 'integral' fault element (intention, knowledge, etc.), and treating D as having foreseen what he would have foreseen sober
Evaluates whether the compromise is defensible in practice (protects public; specific intent offences have basic intent fallbacks, e.g. murder to manslaughter, s18 to s20)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Under DPP v Majewski [1977], evidence of voluntary intoxication may show that D lacked the mens rea of a specific intent offence, such as murder, s18 OAPA 1861 or theft, but not of a basic intent offence, such as manslaughter, s20, s47 or reckless criminal damage. Lord Elwyn-Jones reasoned that getting drunk is a reckless course of conduct supplying the mens rea, and the Lords relied openly on public protection.

The charge of abandoning subjectivism is well founded. Recklessness under R v G [2003] means awareness of a particular risk. Someone who drinks at a party is not thereby aware of a risk of wounding a stranger hours later. Majewski substitutes general earlier fault for specific mens rea at the time of the act, which breaks both coincidence and correspondence.

The charge of incoherence also has force. 'Specific intent' has never been satisfactorily defined.
