R v Heard [2007] treated intentional sexual touching as basic intent, explaining specific intent as offences requiring purpose or an ulterior intent. That shows the labels follow policy rather than analysis. Applications also conflict. In Jaggard v Dickinson [1981] a drunken belief supported a lawful excuse to criminal damage under s5(3). Yet R v O'Grady [1987], R v Hatton [2005] and s76(5) CJIA 2008 deny a drunken mistaken belief in the need for self-defence even on a murder charge.

Further distinctions follow: a drunken intent is still an intent (R v Kingston [1995]), sedatives are treated differently from alcohol (R v Hardie [1985]), and Dutch courage is no defence (AG for Northern Ireland v Gallagher [1963]).

There are alternatives. Full subjectivity (the Australian R v O'Connor (1980)) risks acquitting violent drunks. The Butler Committee (1975) proposed a separate offence of dangerous intoxication, which would label the conduct more honestly. The Law Commission (Law Com No 314, 2009) proposed keeping the basic idea but replacing the labels. Intoxication would remain relevant to 'integral' fault elements such as intention, knowledge and purpose. For other fault elements, D would be treated as having foreseen what he would have foreseen if sober.

The compromise works reasonably well in practice, because most specific intent offences have a basic intent fallback, such as murder to manslaughter or s18 to s20. The statement is nonetheless largely right: the rules rest on policy and imprecise categories, and the Law Commission's integral fault test would at least make the policy open and consistent.

questions.q: Lola has endured years of controlling and violent behaviour from her husband, Max. One evening Max tells her he will 'finish her off' when he returns from the pub, as he has threatened many times before. While he is out, she takes a kitchen knife and hides it under a cushion. When Max returns, drunk, he taunts her about her appearance and tells her their children would be better off without her. She feels overwhelmed, says she 'snapped', and stabs him once in the chest, killing him. A psychiatrist diagnoses Lola as suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and depression at the time. Discuss whether Lola may have a defence to murder.
markScheme: Self-defence: s76 CJIA 2008; was force necessary in the circumstances as she believed them (Williams (Gladstone); Beckford)? Max was not attacking when she stabbed; pre-emptive force allowed (Beckford) but threat must be imminent; force likely unreasonable; Clegg: failure means murder
Loss of control (ss54-56 Coroners and Justice Act 2009): partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter; burden on prosecution to disprove once sufficient evidence (s54(5)-(6))

Loss of self-control need not be sudden (s54(2)); the earlier knife-hiding is evidence of planning and potentially a 'considered desire for revenge' (s54(4)), but preparation for self-protection is not necessarily revenge

Qualifying triggers: fear of serious violence (s55(3)), given his threats; and/or things said constituting circumstances of an extremely grave character causing a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged (s55(4)); the history of abuse is relevant

Objective test (s54(1)(c)): person of Lola's sex and age with normal tolerance and self-restraint in her circumstances; history of abuse forms part of the circumstances, but conditions affecting tolerance and self-restraint are excluded (s54(3))

R v Challen [2019] (decided under the old provocation law, with fresh psychiatric evidence): coercive control and its psychological effects can be relevant to loss of control and diminished responsibility

Diminished responsibility (s2 Homicide Act 1957 as amended): PTSD and depression as recognised medical conditions; substantial impairment (Golds [2016]) of the ability to form a rational judgment or exercise self-control; explanation for the killing (significant contributory factor)
Burden: on Lola for diminished responsibility (balance of probabilities); where uncontradicted expert evidence supports the defence, a murder conviction may be unsafe (R v Brennan [2014])
Interaction: both partial defences can be run together; PTSD relevant to diminished responsibility but excluded from the 'normal tolerance' test for loss of control
Reasoned conclusion: self-defence unlikely; strong case for diminished responsibility; arguable loss of control
questions.modelAnswer:
Self-defence. Under s76 CJIA 2008, Lola is judged on the facts as she genuinely believed them (R v Williams (Gladstone) [1984]), and the force must be reasonable in those circumstances. Pre-emptive force can be lawful (Beckford v R [1988]), but when she stabbed Max he was taunting her, not attacking her. A jury is unlikely to find that stabbing him in the chest was necessary or reasonable then. If it fails, it fails entirely (R v Clegg [1995]).

Loss of control. Under s54 Coroners and Justice Act 2009, murder is reduced to manslaughter if D lost self-control, had a qualifying trigger, and a person of her sex and age with normal tolerance and self-restraint, in her circumstances, might have reacted in the same or a similar way. The loss of control need not be sudden (s54(2)), which helps abused women whose reaction builds over time. Hiding the knife may be presented as planning, or as a 'considered desire for revenge', which excludes the defence under s54(4). It could equally be preparation for self-protection. Lola's fear of serious violence, given Max's threat to 'finish her off', may be a trigger under s55(3). His words, set against years of abuse, may also be circumstances of an extremely grave character giving her a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged (s55(4)). Her history of abuse forms part of her 'circumstances'. However, s54(3) excludes conditions that affect only her general capacity for tolerance and self-restraint, so her PTSD cannot be used to lower that standard, although a mental condition may still be relevant to the gravity of the trigger (R v Rejmanski [2017]). R v Challen [2019], although decided under the old provocation law, shows that evidence of coercive control can be highly relevant. Once raised, the prosecution must disprove it.

Diminished responsibility. Under s2 Homicide Act 1957, as amended, Lola must prove on the balance of probabilities that she had an abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition. PTSD and depression both qualify. She must also show that it substantially impaired her ability to form a rational judgment or exercise self-control, where 'substantially' means important or weighty (R v Golds [2016]), and that it provides an explanation for the killing as a significant contributory factor. Where the psychiatric evidence is unchallenged, R v Brennan [2014] indicates the jury should generally accept it.

Self-defence is unlikely to succeed. Diminished responsibility is Lola's strongest route to a manslaughter verdict, and loss of control should be left to the jury as an alternative.

questions.q: 'The refusal of English law to allow duress as a defence to murder rests on the assumption that the law may demand heroism. That assumption is morally defensible only if the law also provides some other way of recognising the reduced culpability of those who kill under threat.' Discuss.
markScheme: States the law: duress (threats or circumstances) unavailable for murder as principal or secondary party (R v Howe [1987]) or attempted murder (R v Gotts [1992]); Dudley and Stephens (1884) on necessity
Notes R v Wilson [2007]: a 13-year-old acting under his father's threats denied the defence

Explains the rationale in Howe: sanctity of life; the law should not allow a person to choose to kill an innocent to save himself; risk of abuse by terrorists and gangs; ordinary person of reasonable firmness can be expected to resist

Explains the contrasting view that duress is an excuse, not a justification; law should not demand heroism; Lord Wilberforce and Lord Edmund-Davies dissenting in Abbott v R [1977]; DPP for Northern Ireland v Lynch [1975] (previously allowed for secondary parties)
Anomalies: duress available for s18 GBH with intent, yet unavailable if the victim dies (murder via GBH intent); unavailable for attempted murder, though attempt requires intent to kill
Current means of recognising reduced culpability: none as a defence; only sentencing via Schedule 21 Sentencing Act 2020 minimum term; mandatory life sentence prevents meaningful differentiation
Loss of control under s55(3) (fear of serious violence) covers only fear of violence from the victim, so does not cover duress by a third party

Reform: Law Commission (Law Com No 304, 2006) recommended duress be a full defence to murder and attempted murder, with the burden on D; earlier proposals (Law Com No 83 and No 218) also favoured a full defence; some suggest a partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter
Considers comparative or theoretical arguments (e.g. Hart on fair opportunity; excuses theory)
Reasoned conclusion on whether the assumption is defensible and what reform best fits
questions.modelAnswer:
English law denies duress as a defence to murder, whether D is the principal or a secondary party (R v Howe [1987]), and to attempted murder (R v Gotts [1992]). Necessity is likewise no defence to murder (R v Dudley and Stephens (1884)). In R v Wilson [2007] the rule was applied even to a 13-year-old acting under his father's threats.

Howe rested on the sanctity of innocent life and the belief that the law should not let anyone choose to kill an innocent person to save himself. It also relied on fears that terrorists and gangs would exploit the defence, and on the expectation that a person of reasonable firmness should resist. Howe overruled DPP for Northern Ireland v Lynch [1975], which had allowed it for secondary parties.

The opposing view treats duress as an excuse, not a justification. The coerced killer does wrong but deserves less blame because he lacked a fair opportunity to act otherwise, in the sense Hart describes. In Abbott v R [1977] the dissenting judges argued that the law should not demand heroism that ordinary people cannot show. The current rule also produces anomalies. Duress is available for s18 wounding with intent but not if the victim dies, even though murder can be committed with the same intention to cause GBH. It is denied for attempted murder, where no one has died.

This bears out the second half of the quotation. If the law demands heroism, it should at least recognise those who fall short of it, but the current law barely does so. Duress cannot reduce murder to manslaughter. Loss of control under s55(3) covers only fear of serious violence from the victim, not from a coercing third party. The only recognition is in sentencing, through the Schedule 21 Sentencing Act 2020 minimum term, and the mandatory life sentence and the murder label still apply.

The Law Commission (Law Com No 304, 2006) recommended that duress be a full defence to murder and attempted murder, with the burden on the defendant, to address the fear of abuse. A partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter would be a middle course: it would mark the wrong of killing an innocent person while recognising the pressure D was under.

The quotation is persuasive. Insisting on heroism is defensible only alongside a partial defence or a discretionary sentence, and English law currently offers neither.
